speechtext: I wish to inform the House that because of the Minister's statement, the period set aside for Government Orders will be extended for thirty-five minutes, starting at one o'clock.

ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS Ms. Lynn McDonald (Broadview-Greenwood) moved:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to act on urgent environmental issues, especially its failure to negotiate a treaty with the United States to reduce acid rain emissions; its failure to incorporate environmental matters in major economic decisions, despite endorsing the Brundtland Report and the report of the National Task Force on Environment and the Economy; and its failure to effect a clean-up of the toxic wastes contaminating the Great Lakes Basin and the St. Lawrence Seaway.
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is my unhappy duty today as the environment critic for the NDP caucus to move a motion which condemns the Government in no uncertain terms for three major failures.
There could have been others on the list. However, in the interest of focusing on what is of highest concern for Canadians, I specified acid rain, which is a problem across the country where we do not have a treaty and do not seem to be getting closer to one; the case of toxic wastes in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway where we have agreements on water quality but in fact are not seeing any clean-up actually happening; and the case of the World Commission on Environment and Development, the Brundtland Report, where we have an excellent report with dynamic recommendations and a hopeful vision of the future. We have a Government which has endorsed it in principle but is not yet acting it out and, indeed, is violating its major premises in its own economic decision making.
As an Ontario Member I will deal particularly with eastern questions. Later today my colleagues from the West will be dealing with environmental issues in their areas. Certainly the environment is a prime consideration for all Canadians.

March 21, 1988
Supply

All Canadians, even in Western Canada, see acid rain as an urgent issue. To Quebecers, however, the issue of acid rain is particularly pressing. It is environmental problem number one, because of its impact: dying lakes and forests, soil acidification, and also diseases such as cancer and respiratory ailments. In the southern part of Quebec on the American border, there are maple stands where one-third of the trees have died as a result of acid rain.
The federal Government's failure to act is very sad. One must not be too cynical, but I have some doubts about the Government's good will, because while the federal Government was negotiating an agreement on acid rain with the United States, it was also negotiating a trade agreement. It could not insist too much on a strong agreement on emissions that cause acid rain because it was also anxious to sign a trade agreement. The price we pay for this trade agreement is the lack of an agreement on acid rain.
There are other costs involved with this free trade agreement, and I am thinking of jobs, our control over investment and basically, the sovereignty of this country. What is also discouraging about the free trade agreement is the fact that it will have a disastrous impact on the environment if it is implemented. According to the federal Government, the agreement is our most important economic decision in this century. However, the decision was made by the federal Government without any studies of the negative consequences for the environment, and it was taken despite the recommendations of the Report of the World Commission on Environment and Development. The federal Government and the provinces approved the Commission's recommendations that environmental matters be incorporated in economic decisions. However, the first economic decision made by the federal Government and supported by the provincial Government of Quebec was to pursue this trade agreement with the United States without considering possible negative effects on the environment and on our future economic potential.
Quebecers are worried about the quality of their water. In rural areas, we see a degradation of water quality by pesticides. The waters around Montreal are contaminated by runoff from chemical industries in New York state. In some cases, concentrations of toxic substances are higher in Montreal than they are further upstream in the Great Lakes. However, the federal Government refuses to contribute one cent to cleaning up the waters of the St. Lawrence River. Last year, the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) stated that cleaning up the St. Lawrence was the federal Government's first environmental priority for Quebec. Since then, the problem has not diminished but the federal Government's priority no longer exists. Instead of taking action, the federal Minister is giving advice to his provincial counterparts. It is excellent advice: raise water taxes to encourage people to stop wasting water!
I agree that the Province, the City of Montreal, and other Quebec municipalities have a responsibility to waste less and to treat waste, but the federal Government also has a role to play. In fact, this is both a national and international issue. Toxic substances originate partly in the region itself, partly in Ontario and the United States.
It is unfair to exclude Quebec from the Great Lakes water quality agreements. Ontario has received $200 million from the federal Government to fight pollution. Quebec should not be left out. The urgency of this question is demonstrated by the fact that the belugas in the St. Lawrence are dying. They are dying because they eat minute organisms which absorb toxic substances, including dioxins. The death of the whales is a danger signal to us all. Some studies have shown that the rate of cancer and birth defects among the human population of the St. Lawrence North Shore is higher than the Canadian average.
Canada has made some progress in reducing the emissions that cause acid rain, particularly sulphur dioxide, and especially in Quebec and Ontario, the worst offending provinces. The federal Government has not done nearly so well with regard to nitrogen oxide, another important cause of acid rain. At meetings in Geneva attempting to get an international accord on this subject, Canada's role was absolutely shameful. Canada stalled and mimicked the Americans regarding acid rain pollution in Canada, denying the importance of the pollution, wanting more research, and not standing with other more environmentally concerned countries for tough standards and real cut-backs in emissions.
The case of toxic wastes is quite different structurally from the question of acid rain. We have not even begun to get into negotiations with the Americans. In the case of toxic wastes in the Great Lakes there are treaties already. We have had the International Joint Commission, and water quality agreements and studies have accumulated over the decades. The question is not to negotiate any kind of a treaty but a failure to get the existing agreements, which have been amended on the basis of recent research, put into practice. The Great Lakes United's Water Quality Task Force I think puts it very well in looking at this question. It reported:
We were shocked to see many blatant violations of those promises on our tour of the Lakes ... in 1986. Plumes of black contaminants still reach out into the Lakes. Large cities still dump sewage that has only received primary treatment. Industrial smoke stacks still belch contaminants into the air. Old dump sites continue to leak dioxins, PCBs and numerous other insidiously destructive chemicals into rivers and lakes. Agricultural run-off continues to release massive quantities of pesticides and phosphorus-laden fertilizers. Dredging operations still pour toxic sediments into open waters. Every day hundreds of trucks still dump contaminated fill into the lakes.
Citizens are still calling for government to be much more active. It is clear to the Great Lakes citizenry that zero discharge of persistent toxic substances is the only hope for our future.
March 21, 1988

Great Lakes United is quite clear about the problems, and I not think any expert would doubt it. It also points out that the International Joint Commission, to which we name half the members, has all the powers it needs. We do not need new laws or treaties. We need some real force in actual enforcement.
A total of 4.5 million Canadians get their drinking water from the Great Lakes system, specifically Lake Ontario. Only one-quarter of a million Americans do. The problem has not been the priority for the Americans that it has been for us, but it is estimated that 90 per cent of the toxic substances in that water come from American sources. The Niagara River brings in contaminated material and 85 per cent of it flows into Lake Ontario. The Niagara River picks up PCBs, dioxins, metals, and carries those substances into Lake Ontario, and because it is a continuous system, they are carried into the St. Lawrence hitting Montreal and affecting Quebec as well.
Niagara Falls is the world's most spectacular toxic waste tourist attraction and it is sad that we have to look at it that way. Even the spray that greets tourists is contaminated. The contamination is thorough. The water, the sediment, the spray, the fish, the mollusks and algae are affected throughout the system. Two hundred and sixty-one artificial chemicals have been identified. Some cause birth defects and some are carcinogens. These include sewage, DDTs, pesticides, metals, PCBs, and the most deadly toxic substances yet known, dioxins.
In 1985 it was estimated by Environment Canada that nine tonnes of toxic chemicals enter the Niagara River every day. The Niagara River Toxic Committee, which has underestimated the toxic discharge in the past, reports 66 hazardous waste dump sites within three miles of the river, 61 of which are in New York State. As well there are 46 so-called inactive sites, but many of these are leaking. Hyde Park is the most dramatic example.
An estimated nine kilograms of dioxins have been detected seeping out from the Hyde Park site which get into our Great Lakes system and into the food chain. The result, Mr. Speaker? Fish consumption is restricted, obviously a necessary measure but hardly any kind of solution to the problem. This is a chemical time bomb. There are six hectares close to the Niagara River and 70,000 tonnes of chemical waste have been put into it in a 20-year period. Clearly the release of all these toxic substances is a violation of the Boundary Water Treaty.
We have an international Water Quality Agreement which should mean that we move very swiftly to zero discharge of toxic substances. These agreements to reduce discharge are not respected. Federal government action is essential for clean up. Litigation has been tried. Pollution Probe, for example, has tried litigation but it has not been successful. The Americans have a superfund but litigation manages to sidetrack it. The very pathetic progress that has been made so far is just not nearly enough.
Supply
The United States Environmental Protection Agency reported only in January of this year on the six tons a day leaking into the Niagara River. That may yet be an underestimation of the harm that is being caused. I cannot stress that too vigorously. I would hope that the subject of toxic wastes and the necessity for clean-up would be on the agenda for the summit meeting with President Reagan in April. It is an absolutely essential item.
I want to turn to the last part of my motion dealing with the Brundtland Commission report, this absolutely vital, important, encouraging and hopeful document in which Canada took a very important part. Canadians formed a part of the public response to it. Its recommendations are superb.
The introduction of the report deals with the nature of the problem of environmental contamination and the disastrous situation we are in right now because of our developmental practices. It reads:
They may show profits on the balance sheets of our generation, but our children will inherit the losses. We borrow environmentalist capital from future generations with no intention or prospect of repaying. They may damn us for our spendthrift ways, but they can never collect on our debt to them. We act as we do because we can get away with it: future generations do not vote; they have no political or financial power; they cannot challenge our decisions.
That has been the shame of it.
While the federal Government has endorsed the Brundtland Commission recommendations, it immediately violated the most basic premise and recommendation of it in the free trade agreement, and that is to incorporate the environment into economic decision-making. With the trade agreement, we have a continental energy proposal, a requirement to continue to sell energy and other natural products to the Americans, regardless of concerns for conservation. It is a deal that will discourage conservation. It is a deal that will discourage the development of alternatives, the soft energy path. It is a deal that will discourage the development of jobs in areas other than the resource sector, and indeed the Government has bragged about how the resource sector will be more important under this deal.
We are, however, talking about non-renewable resources. The proposal is that we will depend more on resources to which, once they are gone, future generations will have no access whatsoever. The possibility of using those resources by having lower energy prices in Canada to stimulate certain industries that would create more jobs has been lost under the trade agreement.
There is the question of harmonization under the trade agreement in the case of pesticides. What does harmonization mean? The Americans take a different approach to pesticides than we do. Our approach needs improving as well, but theirs is based on a different premise. They allow for a cost benefit trade-off: "We will accept a certain number of deaths from pesticides if there are economic benefits". Our approach talks about unacceptable risks and puts health consequences as

March 21, 1988
Supply
something not to be traded away for dollars. Yet we have abandoned that in the trade agreement.
The Government is still spending more money subsidizing the destruction of the environment than it is repairing and caring for it. In the case of the trade agreement, that trend will continue. The Government has paid lip-service, but it is simply not acting to incorporate the environment into economic decisions, to ensure that we do not simply look at the money made by our forests but at the cost of reforestation as well. When a resource disappears, we must look at the costs involved in revising it.
There is not very much time left. Let me quote briefly from the Brundtland report. It reads:
Industrialized countries must recognize that their energy consumption is
polluting the biosphere and eating into scarce fossil fuel supplies ... But the
process must be accelerated to reduce per capita consumption and encourage a
shift to non-polluting sources and technologies.
Yet the trade agreement wants more of the same. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) would have us sell our easily accessible oil and gas in order to get money to so-called develop or extract and sell off our more inaccessible and costly oil and gas. This is a scandalous misunderstanding of the situation.
I simply want to say, as the Brundtland Commission said, that the time to act is now. I think Canadians are fundamentally fair and reasonable. They do not want to deprive future generations, the children whom they educate and look after, of their environment and the possibility of having livelihoods in the future. I think Canadians are reasonable and want to see action.
I would hope that the Government would stop being so cosmetic in its approach and start looking at the cosmos, become cosmological, not "cosmeticological". I would hope that it would stop taking the public relations approach and would genuinely respond to the public which places a very high priority on the environment.
The Brundtland report does give us cause for hope because it says that it can be done. We do not have to accept poverty along with saving the environment. We can have economic growth and development by incorporating economic decisionmaking into an environmentalist perspective. That is what we must do, but many changes would be required by the Government, including changes in its dealings with the Americans. It must have the political will to serve Canadians and to serve the interests of future generations of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in her remarks on the NDP motion today, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) said that the Government of Canada has endorsed the Brundtland Commission report, the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, but has paid only lip-service to the report itself through its day-to-day actions. Yet, during a visit to the United Nations in New York
on the occasion of the big debate on the Brundtland Commission report, Madam Brundtland, the Prime Minister of Norway, who headed that international commission, singled out Canada for its world leadership in implementing the recommendations of her commission's report.
I ask the Hon. Member, who are the people of Canada to believe on this subject, the NDP or Madam Brundtland?

Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that Madam Brundtland is a very diplomatic person, and it is well known that in diplomacy, one gets further by buttering up the people one is trying to get something from than by condemning them. She is being very diplomatic.
Madam Brundtland should not be treated as being quite separate from the New Democratic Party. She herself is a social democrat and is head of the Labour Party of Norway. I am pleased to see a woman, feminist, socialist and environmentalist in that high office.
The proof of the pudding is in the eating. I hope the Minister will explain to the Canadian people why, under the trade deal, there was not one study, not one SAGIT which looked at this matter. I quoted the Brundtland report directly where it said that we must move to different uses of energy. Yet the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister's colleague, is adamant that using fossil fuels, oil and gas, the non-renewable energy sources, is the path the Government is directed to. That is an absolute contradiction and I am surprised that the Minister cannot see that.

Mr. Speaker, in congratulating the Hon. Member on her fine speech, I would like to ask her if she would expand and elaborate on the question of energy and the trade agreement. She did already touch on it, but I am curious about her thoughts on what the long-term environmental implications are of the trade agreement as it affects energy export. I would like to know of other thoughts she might have on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome that question because it is the energy aspects of the trade deal which are so attractive to the Americans. They have a desire to have access to our non-renewable energy sources, and this deal gives them that unfettered access. If we need to cut back because of some kind of crisis like an oil crisis, which has happened in the past, we will still have to continue supplying the American markets proportionately.
The American market is an enormous market. Americans are very high energy users, as are Canadians. We use 80 times the energy per capita of people in Third World countries, for example. There is no incentive in this deal for us to explore other energy options, to make better use of our energy, to get more out of less, a very, very important aspect of the Brundtland report. That is something we are trying to do in manufacturing, for example, producing more with less use of natural resources.
March 21, 1988

The continental energy approach is absolutely foolish and suicidal. It goes completely against the thrust of the Brundt-land Commission report, which is that we have obligations to future generations. In the case of non-renewable resources, there is simply no opportunity for that undertaking to be respected. The material will be gone and we will even have given up the opportunity of obtaining the spin-off jobs in manufacturing. We have documents given to Ministers which show that non-renewable energy resources are still treated as a surplus in the mistaken mentality of the Government. We have too much of a supply so we have to get access.
I did not mention uranium in my speech, but certainly that is another very important area where the Government wants to ensure Canadian access to the American market. Yet we have no means for disposal of high level radioactive wastes. We have no adequate means of disposal of low level mine tailings. The Minister's department is aware of the concerns, yet there is no action on these wastes, and the prospect is for increased mining of uranium. We are already the world's largest producer and exporter. We even export to France, which is still conducting atmospheric testing of nuclear bombs. It is absolutely unconscionable that we should be involved in that.
The Government's concern is that we have to keep selling more. It welcomes the trade agreement with the U.S. as an opportunity to ensure access to that market. It approaches this issue strictly as a market matter. Yet what will it cost to clean up? If the Government looked at the Brundtland Commission report it would not say, "We can make some money selling uranium to the Americans and French". It would look at the cost of clean-up. Who is going to pay those costs through cancer deaths and birth defects and so on? It is the young people and their children who are going to have to pay the penalty for this very mistaken policy of our present Government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all too often Parliament descends to exaggerated rhetoric and intemperate partisanship. The environment is a field in which neither tone is appropriate. The stakes are simply too high given the extent to which the human race is trashing the planet's life support systems, the air we breathe, the water we drink, the soil that produces our food. What is at issue here for all of us is nothing less than survival. We owe our children and future generations not rhetoric or partisanship but the healthiest possible environment in which to live. Yet this NDP motion is not designed to shed light on the subject. It is designed to discredit genuine efforts to improve the environment.
Nevertheless, Sir, I welcome this occasion to detail the record of the current federal Government in the environmental field. I do so not to score cheap political points but to celebrate a genuine partnership that the federal Government is forging with the provinces, industry, environmental groups, labour, and others committed to environmental protection. Much
Supply
remains to be done and this Government is committed to doing it in concert with our partners.
I think nothing is achieved by denying credit where credit is due. Yet that is what the NDP motion before us does as a substitute for its Party policy. Any non-partisan observer would concede that more has been done to protect the natural environment at the national level over the last three and a half years than during any previous comparable period. The record, unadorned by rhetoric and unembellished by partisanship, speaks for itself. Allow me to put the Government's achievements on the record.
When appointed Minister of the Environment in August, 1985, I said that acid rain was this country's most serious environmental problem. No one can deny that our Government has delivered on its commitment to reduce acid rain-causing emissions from Canadian sources. Last month in Halifax I signed, on behalf of the Government and people of Canada, the last of seven legally binding federal-provincial accords. Together, the accords constitute the most ambitious joint government pollution control program ever launched in Canada. By 1994, the eight-Government pact will slash industry and utility sulphur dioxide emissions by 50 per cent, a remarkable demonstration of national will. The federal Government has committed $150 million to abate acid rain emissions at source, and a further $150 million to advance the technology and research required for the task.
At the same time, we have introduced the toughest national measures in the world to control nitrogen oxide emissions from motor vehicles. Last September, allowable emissions from cars and light-duty trucks were cut by over 60 per cent. In December of this year, allowable emissions from heavy-duty vehicles will be cut by 50 per cent. We are the first country in the world to introduce such tough NOx controls. Our vehicles will now be up to six times cleaner than those of Europe.
Sir, not content to put only our house in order, we have been eager to provide world leadership on the issue. It was, after all, this Government that signed the Helsinki Agreement which committed each signatory country to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions by 30 per cent, a subject in which my friend, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), has such a keen interest.
Opposition Parties can rail against our Government for not yet achieving an agreement with the U.S. to cut the flow of acid rain across the borders of our two countries, but they ignore several facts. First, no previous Canadian Government was able to achieve an acid rain accord with the U.S., either. Success continues to elude acid rain control champions within the U.S. itself.
Second, no previous Canadian Government has given the issue a higher priority than we have. Unlike the Trudeau Government, we have not merely moralized about the issue. We have acted. Witness the strong domestic control program mentioned earlier.

March 21, 1988
Supply
Third, we intend to accelerate our efforts to achieve an acid rain agreement with the U.S. Whether or not we succeed, the Government of Canada cannot be held accountable for the record of another sovereign country in this or any other area of public policy, however much our own environment may be affected. By attacking the Canadian Government on this score, the NDP's motion is as naive as it is unfair.
If acid rain is this country's top environmental problem, and I think it is, toxic chemicals vie for that distinction. Accordingly, our Government has acted to stem the flow of toxics into our environment. A major instrument for doing so is the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, now awaiting action by Parliament at the last stages of debate. The law will consolidate much of the legislative authority of the Minister of the Environment. It will provide a framework to co-ordinate federal and provincial environmental laws. It will manage toxic chemicals through their full life cycle, from research and development to production and entry into the market-place, from transport right through to final disposal as waste. It will also create mechanisms to regulate pollution from the federal Government itself.
The Bill contains the toughest sanctions against polluters ever enshrined in Canadian environmental law, including $1-million-a-day fines and jail terms for corporate offenders.
A panel of top flight environmentalists is already working on a list of priority chemicals so that the law will be ready to be acted upon and enforced immediately upon royal assent.
Toward the same goal, a tough enforcement and compliance program has been devised, and the Government has approved $37 million in new money to apply the law.
While awaiting passage of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the Government is using existing instruments to act on specific pollution problems across the country, focusing in particular on toxic chemical hot spots. A case in point is the $34 million Sydney tar ponds excavation, the biggest of its kind in the history of Canada and the second biggest ever undertaken anywhere in the world.
The clean-up of the Windermere Basin in Hamilton harbour is another example. Such pollution measures are not being taken in a vacuum, but rather in the context of the federal water policy which we released just before Christmas. The policy covers everything from large scale water exports and major water diversion projects, which we have banned, to realistic water pricing, which we have championed.
In the same context, we have updated and fortified the Canada-U.S. Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement in concert with the U.S. Government. Such environmental watchdogs as Great Lakes United, referred to already in this debate, have helped ensure that the new agreement is as comprehensive as it is tough. For the first time, the agreement now covers all sources of Great Lakes pollution and establishes
accountability mechanisms to make sure that specific reduction targets and schedules are actually met.
None of our Great Lakes targets and schedules is more pressing than those written right into the landmark accord signed last year by the Government of Canada with the Governments of the United States, New York State and Ontario. It will reduce toxic loadings into the Niagara by 50 per cent by 1996, the first time the four jurisdictions have ever been able to agree on a specific pollution abatement program for a river that provides drinking water for 4.5 million Canadians.
The Government of Canada is taking the same approach to pollution that threatens the other half of the Great Lakes Basin, the St. Lawrence River. I have been negotiating with my opposite number, Clifford Lincoln, Quebec's Minister of Environment, on a plan to mobilize resources from both Governments. The plan has not yet been completed because it takes time to correct years of neglect and indifference under previous Governments.
However, the St. Lawrence River is a priority of the federal Government, a priority of mine and of my department. If it is a priority of the NDP, as the motion suggests, it is news to everyone in this House and probably to everyone else in Canada, from one coast to the other. To my knowledge, the NDP has never before raised this issue in the House. Certainly, it has never asked me a single question in Oral Question Period on the clean-up of the St. Lawrence River.
Strong as the Government's pollution control program is, I believe future generations will remember the current Government's first mandate, in the environmental sphere, for the leadership it has provided on national parks. From 1972, when the Liberals were in power, until the time we were elected in September, 1984, not a single new national park was established. It was "the dark age" as far as parks were concerned, in the words of one large national environmental group.
Since then the Government has established four new national parks, including Pacific Rim in British Columbia, which we completed only this past week by paying off the $28 million debt for forest lands owed to the Province of British Columbia by the previous Government for 17 years.
The other three new parks are South Moresby, also in British Columbia, at Ellesmere Island in the high Arctic, and at the Bruce Peninsula in Ontario, the country's first ever national marine park under our recently released national marine park policy.
I hope that in the next year national parks will be created in the Saguenay in Quebec, in the prairie grasslands of Saskatchewan, and at Banks Island in the far North. I will be proposing such parks to my cabinet colleagues.
The amendments Cabinet has already approved to the National Parks Act constitute the first overhaul of that law since it was passed more than a half century ago. Those amendments will ensure that all parks, existing parks and ones
March 21, 1988

yet to be established, will be managed by standards that can better conserve rich ecological features while enhancing opportunities for people to appreciate and enjoy them.
Our stress on conservation includes the built heritage, an area almost totally neglected by previous Canadian Governments. The federal-provincial cost sharing agreement to restore historic sites and properties of national significance received a major infusion of new money. By the end of March we will have signed agreements to restore three major landmarks this year alone. They are George Brown House in Toronto, City Market in Saint John, and St. Paul's Anglican Church in Halifax. This is not to mention our cash contribution to the new Marconi Exhibition Centre in Glace Bay, to which the Italian community has also contributed generously.
To prevent the federal Government itself from destroying the country's precious built heritage, new internal mechanisms have been engineered. The approach involves a national registry and tough Treasury Board requirements.
There is another form of heritage that is vital to our country-it is wildlife. Our major priority in this area is the North American Waterfowl Management Plan, a $1.5 billion-15-year program to reverse declining populations in Canada and the United States. The combined contribution within Canada from all sources, including the federal Government, will be $250 million over the course of the program.
I was honoured to sign the plan with the United States Secretary of the Interior, Donald Hodel, in May, 1986. Mr. Hodel and I signed another important bi-national wildlife management plan last summer to protect the 180,000-head porcupine caribou herd in the Yukon-Alaska Range.
As well, this past year Canada established two new national wildlife areas, Polar Bear Pass on Bathurst Island in Northwest Territories and Last Mountain Lake in Saskatchewan.
Equally significant, 11 new RAMSAR sites were designated for wetland protection, bringing Canada's total to 17. That is more than any other country in the world.
With the World Wildlife Fund, Canada has launched two important initiatives. One is the endangered species recovery fund, to which we committed $1 million. The second is the wildlife toxicology Fund, now completing its third successful year after receiving to date $3 million of federal funding. Wildlife will also gain from the money that Cabinet has added to my Department's budget for pesticides management, $16 million over the next five years.
This Government has been among the strongest supporters of the United Nations' World Commission on Environment and Development, the Brundtland Commission, which was referred to earlier in the debate. What is more, we are practising the Brundtland ethic, the sustainable development ethic, by integrating economic and environmental decisions through both programs and funding arrangements.
Supply
Prime Minister Brundtland herself, as I pointed out earlier in my question to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), has singled out Canada as a world leader in implementing the report's recommendations. One of our key responses has been to launch a reform of the federal environment assessment and review process. In the same spirit, we hosted the international conference on ozone depletion, which produced the historic Montreal Protocol last September. That protocol, which constitutes the first-ever global treaty on the atmosphere, will reduce ozone-depleting chemicals by at least 50 per cent by 1999.
We are not simply preaching the Brundtland ethic. We are putting it into practice. We are weaving the Brundtland ethic into the very fabric of our decision-making and our funding.
We will also be hosting the most important international conference ever held on global atmospheric pollution problems at Toronto in late June. The Montreal conference on ozone depletion, and now a broader conference in Toronto at the end of June, dealing with the whole range of atmospheric pollution problems from Arctic haze to the greenhouse effect, to acid rain, to ozone depletion itself, reflect our Government's leadership towards an international law of the air.
Canada is providing leadership right around the globe, bringing nations together at major conferences, mobilizing policy-makers, experts and others, to see whether we can deal with all of these individual problems in a broader context in the form of what I have called an international law of the air, and we are making real progress towards that end.
My speaking time is running out so I cannot put on the record the many other significant accomplishments of the Government. Other government speakers throughout the debate will have to deal with such measures as our anti-leaded gasoline campaign, which will outlaw lead in gasoline by the end of December, 1992. By 1990, about 90 per cent of lead in gasoline will be removed. We have eliminated altogether the disparity in excise taxes on leaded and unleaded gasoline which favoured the more polluting form.
We have undertaken a public information and awareness campaign to sensitize people to the dangers to their own health and to the natural environment posed by misfueling and by tampering with anti-pollution devices. All of these things and others could be mentioned, such as the pivotal role the federal Government played on the National Task Force on the Environment and Economy. These are a credit to this Government and to the country as a whole in the environmental field. I know the speakers who follow me will be detailing them.
For my part, permit me to conclude on this one note. The Government, of which I am proud to be a member, has spent more money on the environment than any previous Canadian Governments. When all the Supplementary Estimates are in for the current fiscal year, those for my own Department and for other departments of the federal Government which are investing heavily in environmental areas under the direction of my Department, the record will speak for itself. But we are

March 21, 1988
Supply
neither complacent nor finished with the job. I urge the New Democratic Party, instead of coming into the House with motions that shroud its own lack of policy, to join us, and I urge other opposition Members to join us in meeting the challenges that remain ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I do have some questions to put to the Minister. I know he had to pad out his address today with a whole lot of subjects that were not in my motion, certainly, I welcome the agreement on the caribou herd in the Porcupine area and the historical sites and things of that sort. However, it is because the Minister did not have enough good things to say about concrete action to get rid of toxic wastes that he went on to these other subjects.
My questions very specifically are, first, this Minister in the area of acid rain is on record as saying that an acid rain agreement with the States would be the litmus test of this Government's ability to negotiate with the Americans. Would he agree that so far his Government has failed the litmus test?
The Minister referred to water policy in his remarks. It is not a statute, it is only a policy. Will he be bringing in legislation? Specifically, will he bring in federal legislation to have drinking water standards, not mere guidelines, but standards for federal lands, including Indian reserves? Is it indeed true that the federal Government does not want to do this because it knows that the quality of the drinking water on so many Indian reserves is abominable and would fail any reasonable standards?
The Minister mentioned a number of bits and pieces of a strategic plan in his own Department. Is it not true that his own Department has abandoned having a strategic plan on the environment? Something I raised in my remarks that the Minister did not address was the subject of toxic wastes. Will the serious subject of removal of toxic wastes, actual excavation and containment in the Hyde Park site, be on the agenda for the summit meeting with President Reagan, or will any of the other toxic waste sites be on the agenda?
I would really like the Minister to address the question of a very important matter in the Brundtland Commission report, that is, the greenhouse effect, the possibility of really major climate changes from many sources, but particularly from the burning of fossil fuels. Has his Department really looked seriously at this problem and does it have any idea as to what the long-term consequences will be of this continued policy of focusing on fossil fuels for our energy?

Mr. Speaker, I have just spoken on the Hon. Member's motion for the past 20 minutes. I would probably need an hour to respond to the half a dozen questions she has put to me, any one of which would probably take longer than the time we have for the entire question period associated with my speech.
The Hon. Member says I padded my speech with references to the Government's record in areas outside her motion. Her motion reads:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to act on urgent
environmental issues, especially its failure to-
It then cites a few issues, by way of example. Does that imply that the very items to which she referred in her question, and which she has lambasted me for including in my speech, are not priorities of the New Democratic Party? Are such things as the North American Waterfowl Management Plan, the declining populations of waterfowl, especially in western Canada, not a priority of the NDP? Does she imply that the NDP is not interested in the built heritage? I thought the Hon. Member was a spokesperson for the NDP on cultural matters a while ago. What could be more important to the culture of the country than the built environment in which we live and work, the physical expressions of the heart and soul of this country as reflected in our buildings and other cultural sites for which I, as Minister, am responsible? I think I can refer with some pride, on behalf of the Government as a whole, to the things we have done with the provinces and with heritage groups across the land, in this field.
The Hon. Member lambastes me for including a reference to national parks in my speech. I can see why the Opposition would not want a Minister of the Crown to refer to the federal Government's record in this field. It is exemplary. But we are not self-satisfied. We are not content. Over the course of many years we have managed, as a country, to complete only half of the total national park system. As I said earlier, during the 14 years prior to our coming into power, not a single new national park was established. How can Canada complete the national park system if, for a decade and a half of Liberal administration, not a single new national park was created? Someone will have to redress that imbalance. If we do not do it as a genuine Conservative Government, as a conservation Government, then no one will do it, at least not with the priority we attach to it.
The Hon. Member asks me about our water policy, the national water policy, the first-ever water policy brought down by the Government of Canada. It includes the full range of issues such as water exports, interbasin diversions, pesticides, toxic chemical controls and all such issues. She went on to ask me whether we will back it up with legislation. We already have the legislative authority. What has been lacking under previous Governments has been the will to take those legal instruments and use them. We are exercising that political will, and we are using the available instruments.
The Hon. Member refers to the excavation of the Great Lakes sites, the so-called hot spots such as Love Canal, Hyde Park, S Site, 102nd Street, and so on. Those hot spots, those industrial waste sites, are included now in the agreement itself, thanks to the broadening of the Canada Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. We are taking an ecosystem approach. We are not concentrating only on this site, that problem or this hot spot or another. We are saying that any assault on the Great Lakes system is a candidate for action by the Government of Canada with our partners, including the Government
March 21, 1988

of Ontario. All sources, among them the sites to which she has made reference, are now included in the agreement.
With respect to acid rain, no previous Government has attached the kind of importance that we have to solving this issue, both domestically and with the United States. In previous years, the policy of the Party of the Hon. Member and that of the Party of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was simply to go down to Washington, lambaste the Americans, bang one's head on the desk, moralize, fingerpoint and all the rest of it. But we did not have the clean hands that brought to the negotiating table the kind of credibility and moral authority that made us effective. We now have those clean hands.
We are saying to the Americans, "Look, we have cleaned up our act. We are reducing by 50 per cent by 1994, based on 1980 figures, acid rain-causing emissions from industry and from utilities. We are spending half a billion dollars a year, and we will be doing so for every year up until 1994 when our progress will have been made".
In fact, by fortifying our case in that fashion we can hold our head high. We can point the finger and say to our American counterparts, "You do the same. You follow suit. Fifty per cent of our acid rain is from your country". In areas such as the Haliburton area of Ontario and Parry Sound-Muskoka, the percentage is closer to 75 per cent.
We can go to the Americans. We can point a finger. We can lecture them on their problems. We can call for a targeted and scheduled approach to acid rain because we have taken exactly that approach within our own country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recognize the Hon. Member for Davenport on a short question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a brief question which goes back to the exchange in the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry within the context of the Brundtland report and the report on the economy and the environment. I asked the Minister whether on free trade he would have any study that would be launched that would be relevant to the negotiations that were taking place at that time. At that time the Minister replied stating that the free trade negotiations and environmental questions are separate and that they should not be linked.
Would the Minister like to elaborate on the answer that he gave in light of the experience he has had since November, 1986?

Mr. Speaker, one of the myths associated with the free trade debate, perpetuated on the floor today by some of the earlier comments of opposition Members, is that Canadians will lose their environment and their capacity to take steps to protect the environment on the high altar of free trade. Nothing could be further from the truth. Implied in the myth is that American environmental standards are much lower than those in Canada and that the free trade agreement
Supply
will harmonize the environmental regimes of the two countries in favour of the lower standard, which is American.
First, there will not be any such harmonization. We could not do it even if we wanted to, and we do not. Laws in both countries, in states and in provinces and at the national level on both sides of the border, have developed in response to particular problems on either side of the border that are indigenous to the area in which the laws are being enforced. We could not have continent-wide environmental standards any more than we could have continent-wide laws. They have to be born of the culture, the geography, the climate and the other circumstances of the jurisdiction in question.
Even if there were to be such a harmonization, and there will not be under free trade or under anything else, the fact remains that it is not true that American standards in every case, or even in most cases, are weaker than those in Canada. For example, when our Government was elected in September of 1984, NOx emissions, about which the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood waxed so eloquent, were three times more stringent in the United States than in Canada. But, because of action by this Government, the NOx emission standards for heavy-duty motor vehicles are currently the strongest in the world. That was accomplished at a time when the same Government of Canada was negotiating an acid rain agreement with the United States.
Given the federal Government's record that I have detailed on the floor of the House of Commons in the environmental field over the past three and a half years, where is the evidence that our efforts toward free trade have in any way circumvented our capacity to act on environmental matters? It has not. We have acted.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the mover of this motion, for it is very well drafted and timely. We are also very glad to take part in this debate.
At the same time, I should like to emphasize the fact that, on behalf of our party, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) will participate in this debate and deal quite eloquently with the environmental issues concerning the St. Lawrence River and the Province of Quebec, focusing on the situation of the St. Lawrence River.
Later this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) will present the views of our party on the environmental vision of Western Canada.
The motion is well drafted, and as I said, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mrs. McDonald).

The debate is very timely. It lends itself to a variety of inputs. Half an hour ago the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) chastised the NDP for having written such a motion. He claimed that in Parliament we were descending to

March 21, 1988
Supply
excessive rhetoric and partisanship. To my astonishment he then launched himself indulgently into an orgy of rhetoric and a very amusing display of selective memory bouts, which must be excused considering the partisan nature of this place. But they were amusing in contrast with the warnings on the part of the Minister that we should not have excesses of rhetoric in this place. I wonder if we have here an example of preaching in one way and practising in another.
I will give the House an example of this type of selective memory bout of the Minister a few moments ago. The 1985 Helsinki Protocol, of course, was signed in 1985. It was made possible by actions taken by the Government of Canada long before the Minister was appointed to Cabinet, and long before the Government was elected.
I will refer to the notion of national parks by refreshing the Minister's memory as to the fact that the vast majority of national parks in Canada were created by successive Liberal Governments. I would also refresh the Minister's memory as to the fact that NOx, on which he waxed eloquently a few moments ago, the public consultations and those measures were launched in 1984. The reality of political life being what it is, it allows the Progressive Conservative Party to reap the political benefits, and that is only fair game. It is only this indulging that is rather peculiar.
Whenever the Conservative Government brought to a conclusion Liberal initiatives that were launched before it was elected, it did reasonably well, and when it departed, it did badly. There is the classic example of abandoning Canada's global role on acid rain. The Conservative Government found enough energy to drag itself to Helsinki and sign the protocol, but in all fairness, since that time there has not been leadership given by the Government on acid rain, on S02 cuts, or on NOx. We learned from Geneva last month on the cutting of car emissions and pursuit of an international protocol that would serve Canada well that the Government is taking its cues from the United States, which is not a sign of great leadership, at least these days.
We have to move ahead in this debate and abandon an approach of exchanges of this nature, but I think it adds to the cut and thrust of the debate for the moment, and I am sure that nobody minds that. Actually, it is good to weave notions that are raised in the course of the debate rather than to start from a prepared text which has little relevance to what has been said before.
I was struck by the intervention of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) and by the motion. It seems to me that it hits on the major points with which the Canadian public is presently preoccupied, and with which the Government ought to be preoccupied.
The fact of the matter is, and I wish to tackle the first item in the motion, that on acid rain, that after three summits, and three and a half years later, we have nothing to point at. The
Government made some serious tactical mistakes in embracing the envoy's report. At that time, the answer of the Government should have been to say that, if the United States wished to conduct its clean-coal technology programs, that is fine. It was announced as a $5 billion program. But we Canadians want the United States to sign an agreement. That is what we want. That message was lost. It was not registered. I know that in January, 1987, for the first time the Minister spoke of a specific negotiation identifying the 4 million tonnes of pollution that crosses the border, but he was alone in that. He was not supported by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Prime Minister got lost in the summits. Three have been held, we are at the eve of a fourth, and somehow we have been sidetracked by the novelty of the clean-coal technology program. What has been spent so far under the auspices of that particular program is $50 million in 1988. That is the extent of the money that has been invested under that particular heading, which raised enormous expectations among Canadians, and which in 1986 was heralded as a substantial breakthrough.
In a few weeks there will be the fourth summit in Washington. Inevitably, the words expressed in this Chamber by President Reagan that he will consider acid rain must be followed up by the Prime Minister. On that score, I once again urge the Minister of the Environment and the Cabinet to prepare the elements for a bill for damage suffered in Canada from acid rain emissions and pollution that comes across the border. Every year this sum is a substantial one to cover damage to monuments, structures, fisheries, forestry, agriculture, and even to human health. We have now reached a point, without having to be strident, without losing our patience, when we must talk the language that is well understood in Washington, which is the language of damage.
As I have pointed out to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark)-but not to the Minister, unfortunately, because when I asked my questions we have not been in the House at the same time, not because of neglect on his part, of course, but because of the day of the week-this matter has to be pursued in economic and monetary terms. We are being damaged. We are downwind from that damage. We have launched a program with a very important set of signatures between the Government of Canada and seven provinces, to which the Minister alluded. Again, this initiative goes back to the time long before this Government was elected. Now we are launching something that will benefit the American economy. It is only fair, if Washington does not reciprocate with a similar parallel program that will provide relief to our natural resources and to our economy, that it should compensate Canada for the yearly damage suffered as a result of transboundary pollution of sulphur dioxide.
In pursuing the question of toxic chemicals in the Great Lakes, there have been many good statements made by the Government and by the Minister, in particular, but little action. The problem is that the Government mercilessly cut the budget of the Canadian Wildlife Service with the Wilson statement of November, 1984. The Canadian Wildlife Service
March 21, 1988

is engaged in a very delicate and important role in establishing toxic chemicals in the Great Lakes. Despite the fine statements, the Government eliminated from the plans and the programs of Ottawa the creation of a Toxicology Centre in Ontario. Those two factors alone are bad enough, but they are made worse by the performance of the Government in relation to the budget of Environment Canada. The performance of the Government in relation to that budget is, to borrow a phrase used earlier, the litmus test of the real intent of the Government in the environment.
No matter how many letters the Minister of the Environment writes to the Toronto Star outlining the $106 million that may be spent over the next eight years on South Moresby to create a park, no matter whether the Minister makes reference to the $150 million-in 1982 dollars, which should tell one when that decision was made-that will be spent over the next 10 years on acid rain abatement technology, as the Minister mentioned a moment ago in the debate, the fact remains that this year that Department is the loser in the budget allocation. It does not even keep pace with the rate of inflation.
If we total, as I have on several occasions in committee for the benefit of the Minister, the losses due to inflation year after year since 1984 when the Government came into power, we find a substantial loss of over 17 per cent or an amount in the neighbourhood of $70 million over the last 3.5 years to 4 years. This has resulted in losses in personnel to the tune of some 336 individuals, be they scientists, technicians, or support people. This 17 per cent loss has resulted in a reduction in the capacity of Environment Canada to pursue programs, to amplify its programs, to amplify its research, and to do the very things which the Government claims that it wants to do.
This is why the accusation is made, quite rightly, that there has been a lot of cosmetics. Public relations on the part of the Government have been pretty good. They have tended to create an impression of action but they have not been substantiated or supported by fact, and the budget of Environment Canada is proof of it.
For the Minister to claim the $150 million which will be spent over 10 years by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, or the $106 million on South Moresby, is another exercise in smoke and mirrors. Canadians will see through it, if they have not already done so, and will give a message to the Minister. They are enormously frustrated by the silence of the Government in relation to the call which has been made many times by the Canadian Federation of Municipalities, asking for help in the construction of badly needed infrastructure related mostly to water. There is a phenomenal backlog, and the Government has been saying "no" to the municipalities. At the same time as the Minister points his finger to problems in the St. Lawrence and in some cities, the federal Government disappears into a beautiful cosmetic cloud. As I said, this creates impressions.
Supply
The Minister made a reference to CEPA, a piece of legislation that has been in the works for some time. It is a good step in the right direction. The problem with the Bill is the Minister himself. It is the classical case of the mouse that roared. An enormous smoke-screen was created, indicating that the Bill would clean up the St. Clair River and the Niagara River, that it would deliver miracles. The fact of the matter is that the content of the Bill, as approved by the Conservative majority on the committee, is weaker than originally promised. All the things the Bill would not do would be the subject of another 20-minute speech. The money allocation behind CEPA-and here we have another Achilles heel-amounts to $37 million over five years, divided by three departments. Once we analyse it we see that the allocation of funds behind the Bill is pretty weak.
The Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement was re-signed, and no doubt the wording was improved. However, where is the political will to implement it? Again I make reference to the fact that the Minister has not been able to command the funds needed to do the job which he promised that he wanted to do. We have not seen, up until now, an indication by the Government that it will implement the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. Not one specific step has been funded since the signing of the new agreement.
The much heralded Niagara work plan is already behind schedule. One reason given is that the Government of Canada is one of the primary culprits in not providing adequate resources or the people needed to do the job. Again, action is missing, but there is much rhetoric, and the gap is becoming greater and greater.
The Quebec Government has announced a $3 billion cleanup scheme along the St. Lawrence River and has been knocking at the door of the Government for some help, for it to match that sum or at least come up with some funds. So far the answer has been "no". We have Quebec at $3 billion and the Government of Canada at zero.
In addition to the budgetary deficiencies of the Government and the losses due to inflation, other very important considerations must be made, namely, the fact-and this was proven in the exchange a few minutes ago-that the Government has completely missed the importance of the impact in the long term on the environment of the free trade negotiations and agreement.
During the negotiations we asked in the House whether or not studies were being conducted on the environmental impact of the free trade agreement, and the answers were negative. I raised the matter in committee and received the answer that I quoted in the exchange with the Minister a few minutes ago. It is astonishing that conceptually the Government would not be capable of putting two and two together. In committee on November 25, 1986-and I quote from the committee proceedings-the Minister said: "Freer trade negotiations and environmental questions are separate and they should not be linked". My goodness. Has the Minister read the chapter on

March 21, 1988
Supply
pesticides in the free trade agreement? They are linked. Idas the Minister read the section dealing with the energy agreement? The linkage is there, and unfortunately it is massive. Therefore, the depth of commitment of the Government to the environment is shallow and superficial when we match it with the policy that it is implementing.
One must register in a debate like this one the necessity for the Government to come to its senses and see that the trade agreement will also impinge on the ability of the Government and future Governments to pass and enforce regulations protecting the environment which may be stronger than those south of the border. In future there could be Canadian industries making representations to the Canadian Government of the day asking to be relieved or asking for weaker regulations. They could claim that they need weaker legislation in order to compete with the same industries south of the border which may not be under environmental regimes at all or may be under weaker ones.
I catch your signal, Mr. Speaker, and therefore I reluctantly relinquish the floor. I thank you for your patience.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions and comments I will recognize the Hon. Minister first, followed by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald).

Mr. Speaker, when all is said and done, the three Parties in the House of Commons probably see eye to eye on what are the major problems in the environmental field in Canada. If the truth be known, I doubt that much separates us on how we approach the different problems on which we are agreed.
What counts is whether a Government acts when it has an opportunity to act. In my speech I detailed, with some substantial documentation, how in a very short time we have acted in the environmental field, without implying that all the problems are resolved or that there was any cause for complacency. There is not.
One of the most important issues with which the three Parties must wrestle is the call of the Brundtland Commission to integrate economic and environmental decision making.
I have a question for the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), who was the former Minister of the Environment. How does he reconcile what seems to be an inherent contradiction in the position of his Party on the subject? On the one hand, the Member embraces the Brundtland ethic that we should integrate environmental and economic decision-making and weave such an integration into the very fabric of everything we do. You cannot just embrace an ideology or a doctrine or a theology. In government, your position has to be reflected in mechanisms and budgetary figures. On the other hand, the Member lambastes the Government because many of our environmental expenditures are in the name of the Brundtland ethic outside the Department of the Environment
but within the federal system under the leadership of the Department of the Environment. The Sydney Tar Ponds is a $37 million clean up, of which 70 per cent is from the federal Treasury through the budget of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. In this case the figures did get reflected in my Department's budget, but in other cases, they did not. Fifty per cent of the $106 million that will be spent by the federal Government on South Moresby does not come from my Department. It will not be reflected in my Estimates but will appear instead in the Estimates of the Minister responsible for western diversification.
The same is true of the acid rain program. There is $150 million for abatement and $150 million for clean-coal technology and for other research and development projects for acid rain. Those are environmental expenditures. They are no less so because they are recorded in the budgets of other departments. When the Member from Davenport totals what our Government has spent in the environmental field, he ignores literally tens of millions of dollars merely because they are outside the Main or Supplementary Estimates of the Department of the Environment. How does the Member reconcile that contradiction, Mr. Speaker? If we are going to integrate the economy and the environment, it has to be reflected in our budgeting. Yet when we do reflect it, the Member dismisses out of hand the importance of such expenditures. There is an inherent contradiction there. Would he rise in the House today and reconcile the irreconcilable?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is a desperate attempt on the part of the Minister to turn a disgrace into a virtue. He keeps trotting out the same two tired horses. One is the South Moresby $106 million expenditure over eight years, and the other one is the $150 million over 10 years, a technological item which is in another department. Beyond that the Minister is short of breath and has to rely heavily on rhetoric.
Here we have a Department that has lost 17 per cent to inflation since 1984.
That is not true.

We have checked it several times and I urge the Minister to use his arithmetic, which is probably as good as mine, and he will have to come to that conclusion if his Department is frank with him. Having lost 17 per cent, he has also lost, over the years, 336 employees, so-called person-years. That is quite an important loss, I submit. Unless the Minister can tell us whether these 336 technicians, scientists and support people have emerged in other departments, we have to conclude that the 336 have been lost. At the same time-and this is something on which the Minister may want to reflect- Environment Canada is receiving a budget increase of 3.6 per cent, but the average government increases have gone up across the board by 8 per cent. What about this one? The budget for National Defence is going up by 8.3 per cent. If you look at the National Defence's basic budget, an increase of 8.3 per cent means an increase of $800 million, which is more than
March 21, 1988

the present budget of Environment Canada. The increase to one department this year entails a sum which is greater than what Environment Canada will receive this year. Maybe there are environmental measures in the Department of National Defence. I would like to hear the Minister give us some examples.
I will give him another example. The Department of Communications' budget went up by 11 per cent. Maybe there are environmental measures in there. Perhaps the Minister could let us know. What about the Department of Finance? Its budget went up by 13.5 per cent this year. Could the Minister tell us more about environmentalists in the Department of Finance who are carrying out environmental projects as a result of this increase?
The budget of the Department of Transport, even that old horse called the Department of Transport, is going up 7.5 per cent. Would the Minister tell us where the environmental initiatives and programs are that will be made possible by the increase of 7.5 per cent in the Department of Transport? Perhaps I will give the Minister a hint and thus be helpful. He should look perhaps at the Department of Agriculture. There the budget has gone up by 24 per cent. That isn't bad, is it? Maybe there are some environmental projects which the Minister can find, and I will be glad to hear from him. If the Minister is implementing the spirit of Brundtland, let the Minister make a statement in the House of Commons one of these days and tell us where in the Department of Agriculture the 24 per cent increase includes environmental measures.
I have another hint for the Minister. The budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has gone up by 23 per cent. Maybe there is something there to help shore up the Minister's fragile political argument today here in the House. The fact remains that until the Minister comes up with the facts, his Department is at the bottom of the list, with an increase of 3.6 per cent, which is less than the inflation rate. Every pensioner in Canada knows what happens to you when you lose ground to inflation.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the intervention by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). Certainly his correcting the record on the budget is helpful. It is important to look at cost of living increases and what is happening in other government departments as well.
I have a couple of questions for the Member. He, of course, is a former environment Minister, and the present Minister was quite within his right to point out some of the failures of the previous Liberal Government.
I would like particularly to ask the Hon. Member to address the Brundtland report in the area of energy. Would he not consider that our reliance on fossil fuels does pose some problems? Is it not time to rethink that? His own Government was pretty lax when it came to looking at soft energy alternatives, renewable energy alternatives. There was some rhetoric, but in terms of firm commitments, budgets and action, it was
Supply
really not very good. Would he consider himself challenged by the Brundtland report, effects on climate change, the greenhouse effect, reliance on fossil fuels?
Another major energy question I would like the Member to look at is that of uranium. His Government was very much involved in the development of uranium. That is an area in which we cannot do what the Brundtland Commission says and incorporate the full environmental costs into economic decision-making because we do not know what the costs are. We know they would be horrendously high.
Would the Hon. Member look at the question of uranium? How do we have sustainable development with a non-renewable resource and with an energy use, uranium, which has such an enormously long period of disposal time which has to be costed and paid for in the future? How does he respond to the Brundtland report in those areas?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) has a consistent habit of raising difficult questions. I do not know whether I can do justice to them in a short time.
Of course there have been failures by previous Liberal Governments. We are all capable of that, even Liberals. I would like to stress something that clearly sticks in my mind because I happened to be in the House at the time. Maybe this precedes the time of the Hon. Member. The then Minister of Energy, the Hon. Alistair Gillespie, announced in 1978 a five-year program on renewable energy incentives, stimulants and you name it, of $400 million. It was to promote all forms of what at that time was termed solar and biomass technology and it was a substantial breakthrough, or so we thought at that time. When the five years were up, it was pretty close to election time and we were looking forward to having that torch carried by the present Government.
Unfortunately, the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of November of 1984 dashed our hopes. We have not seen any effort made on renewable energy through the NRC or other agencies ever since. As a matter of fact, two programs which were intended to conserve energy, CHIP and COSP, were eliminated in 1985.
The soft energy path and its objectives is a very relevant issue. Perhaps we should have done more, but certainly we did not neglect it. At that time, we did not know the name Brundtland. The theology had not yet emerged as clearly as it has now, but certainly anyone who links energy with environmental issues, as the Hon. Member frequently does, is putting the finger on the very core of what environmental safety for the globe is all about. That is where the major impact is made. It comes from energy, and we must watch those policies like hawks in addition to watching the policies of transport, agriculture and the like.

March 21, 1988
I do not want to say something that the Hon. Member knows already, but she may not know about the $400 million that was approved for the soft energy path in 1978 by the then Minister of Energy.
The other big question the Hon. Member raised on uranium as a source of energy and sustainable development is one that we have not been able to finalize in our thinking. We know that our dependence on nuclear electricity is actually increasing. We are faced here with an interesting dilemma because we know that in the short term electricity produced by nuclear energy is non-S02 polluting. It does not contribute to acid rain.
It is actually a source of dismay to us when we learn that a nuclear station must be shut down for repairs and a coal-powered station must be activated in its place. We all know that that means additional S02 pollution, at least in Ontario, by Ontario Hydro, as we have learned in recent weeks. But we know also that in the long term the uncertainty and the cost of disposal involved with uranium waste are enormous and are not properly taken into account by long-term decision-makers.
On that issue, we are ambivalent, or at least ambiguous. I do not have a final answer for that question because of this dichotomy and the conflict between the short and the long term. I would hope that we could accelerate as an alternative our research on fusion and come up sooner than predicted with the production of alternative energy that may be environmentally friendly though not nuclear for the benefit of generations to come.

LANDING OF FISH IN CANADA-CONSULTATION SOUGHT ON NEW REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fish processing industry must deplore the Conservative Government's decision meekly to accept the GATT panel ruling against Canadian regulations on the export of unprocessed fish. speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: SOFTWOOD LUMBER EXPORTS-PAYMENT OF TAX BY SECONDARY MANUFACTURERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, federal cabinet Ministers from British Columbia, for reasons known only to themselves, continue to take actions which harm the interests of that province. On Friday I pointed out how the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), who is from British Columbia, mistreated the B.C. sports fishing industry. We all remember the foolish decision of the Minister to impose a 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber exported to the United States instead of fighting the decision through GATT or before the U.S. Interstate Commerce Commission. That 15

per cent tax has now been incorporated as a permanent part of the Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement.
As if that were not bad enough, the Minister has forced 25 independent secondary softwood lumber manufacturers to pay the tax, while 20 other producers do not because they were certified for exemption. After more than a year of negotiations with the federal Government, those producers, known as the Coalition of Secondary Softwood Lumber Manufacturers, have been forced to take their own Government to the Federal Court of Canada.
If the Minister has any sense of fairness at all she will settle this case out of court and award compensation to those 25 Canadian producers who have been unfairly discriminated against as a result of the Minister's sheer incompetence.

He reached out and touched many people during his life. He is survived by his wife Ruth and daughter Judith. I ask all parliamentarians to join with me this afternoon in extending our sympathy to Mrs. Bell and Judy. Canada has lost a great Canadian.

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-ANNIVERSARY OF THE SHARPEVILLE MASSACRE
SOUTH AFRICA-ANNIVERSARY OF THE SHARPEVILLE MASSACRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today marks the 28th anniversary of the Sharpeville massacre in South Africa.
In March, 1960, the Pan Afrikanist Congress launched a peaceful campaign to demonstrate against a law requiring blacks to carry passbooks.
A group of several thousand gathered on March 21 in Sharpeville to stage a peaceful protest. Without warning, the South African police opened fire on the crowd, killing 69 and wounding 200. Among them were men, women, and children.
The brutality of this event sent a shockwave through the international community, catapulting the South African question onto the international stage and drawing the world's attention to the racist practices in that country.
The South African Government responded to the criticism, not with reform, but with further suppression. A state of emergency was declared and the African National Congress and the Pan Afrikanist Congress were banned.
Twenty-eight years have passed, but, sadly, not much has changed.

Mr. Speaker, people used to believe an old saying: "As good as money in the bank". However, that can mean today no money at all because it is possible for a bank to confiscate an inactive account if it is below a certain balance and after a certain period of time.

My purpose in making this statement is to give the advice that anyone with a small account that has not had much activity lately should check to see if he has anything in the bank at all. He may have less than what he started with.

subtopic: THE YUKON-SETTLEMENT OF LAND CLAIMS URGED
THE YUKON-SETTLEMENT OF LAND CLAIMS URGED
speechtext:
