The House resumed consideration of the motion of Ms. McDonald:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to act on urgent environmental issues, especially its failure to negotiate a treaty with the United States to reduce acid rain emissions; its failure to incorporate environmental matters in major economic decisions, despite endorsing the Brundtland Report and the Report of the National Task Force on Environment and the Economy; and its failure to effect a clean-up of toxic wastes contaminating the Great Lakes Basin and the St. Lawrence Seaway.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this very important debate and want to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for bringing it forward.
The debate today has to go beyond simply condemning the Government for its inaction in the area of the environment. While we can condemn the Government for its failures, and those failures are real and serious, we need to move beyond that and look at the entire system. Twenty years from now people who read this debate will probably remark on how timid on all sides of the issue we were, how slow we were to state the truth about what is happening in our environment and how blind we were to the reality of the environment. In many ways we, on all sides of the House, are children of our times. Operating within this present system we can have better or worse governments. The record of this present Government we have to admit is abominable.
We can begin back in 1984 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed his first Minister of the Environment, a Minister who admitted she knew nothing about the environment and her attitude showed that she could not care less. The fact that she was appointed indicates very clearly that the Prime Minister himself knew little about the environment and cared less. Since that time we have had a series of cut-backs. We now have 336 fewer employees in the Department of the Environment than we had in 1984 and $71 million less is available to the Department of the Environment, important as that is supposed to be in Canadian policy. We can admit though that the present Minister is both knowledgeable about the environment and committed to it, but he is playing catch-
Supply
up. He is behind the ball all the time. He is not getting the kind of support from his cabinet colleagues that he should get.
Perhaps the most obvious example has been illustrated here by previous speakers, namely, the failure of the Prime Minister to stand up for Canadian interests on acid rain. Instead he is trying to reach some cosy arrangement with President Reagan, something to satisfy the President and to reinforce the buddy-buddy system which the Prime Minister has with the American President. This is not satisfactory as far as Canadian interests in the whole area of acid rain are concerned.
What about our fisheries policy? Here the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) has brought in a policy of trading off one part of the environment for enhancement in another. He calls it "the no net loss policy" "or the enhancement policy". It involves selling off part of our environment with the idea that it can be compensated for by enhancement in some other part. The kinds of problems we find in Canada are found in a magnified way in the developing world where, in the attempt to pay their debts and meet the requirements of the international monetary system, they are forced into a plantation economy. Most of us, when we were kids, if we grew up in a family with more than one or two children, were aware of how you have to be very careful when dividing a pie. We used to have a method where one person would divide and the other person would get first choice. We do not do that in the international system, we divide and we get first choice.
However, if we did have fairer shares, then the problem, a lot of people say, is that no one would have enough. With five billion people in our world it would simply mean that everyone would have a standard of poverty. As a result, for a long time people have been talking about a bigger pie. The idea is that we will both get more pie, but my share will always be bigger than your share even if I cannot eat all of my share. The problem with that, of course, is that if we keep making bigger and bigger pies we will very soon run out of ingredients. The side effect of my keeping a larger and larger share for myself is that I will soon have so much uneaten pie kicking around that it is going to start going bad, attracting flies and rats, and we will be buried under the pollution of our share of affluence, which is now happening to a large extent in North American and western Europe.

Mr. Speaker, I have sat in this Elouse on both sides and come to the conclusion that Opposition Days are an opportunity to rise to the heights of hyperbole, regardless of which side you are on. One side condemns the Government, the other side praises the Government. One side says we are facing a crisis, the other side says we do not have a problem at all. One side says you have done nothing, the other side says we have done everything. We have certainly had enough of that today. I commend the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) who has brought this motion to the floor. It is right that this House and this country focus its attention on the challenge to our environment and focus its attention on the imperative need for a solution. I welcome this debate and hope that there may come out of it not something as silly as condemning the Government or as facile as to say there is nothing wrong, but that we can think together both for today and the future about the possibilities we have as Members of Parliament.
First, we must recognize that we are not only the victims, but part of the problem as a human race. As the Brundtland report makes abundantly clear, one of the fundamental causes for the environmental crisis facing humanity is simply the growth of the human race at such a rapid rate in the past few years and the urbanization of the vast majority of humanity, particularly in developed areas. For instance, three out of every four persons live in an urban community which is no longer rightly described in the term "city".
I grew up in the City of Toronto when it was a city of some
700,000	people, with clearly defined borders. One could leave it very quickly to get into the rural countryside. Today, the City of Toronto is surrounded by cities such as my own Scarborough, Mississauga, and other cities in their own right which stretch for 100 miles, from Oshawa around the west end of Lake Ontario to Niagara Falls. It stretches up into Cambridge, Kitchener and ultimately to the City of London.
This is a Canadian example of a world-wide phenomenon, namely the replacement of the city by conurbation, which is the congregating of urban municipalities which often stretch for hundreds of miles. An example of this would be the area from north of Boston to south of Washington or, in the
instance of the Great Lakes, from west and north of Chicago to the east end of Lake Ontario. The result of that all over the world is a threat to the purity of the environment and the survivability of the atmosphere.
The first lesson we should learn from this is that it is not a local or regional problem, the fault for which can be linked to this person, that party or that group. It is not an ideological problem. When we consider the world situation, we find that this prevalence of conurbations and the accompaniment of pollution exists regardless of whether it is a private enterprise system, a socialist system, democracy or communism. It exists regardless of the factors to which we often look for reasons.
The fact is that there are two reasons for these conurbations. One is the rapid growth of humanity in the past 40 years and the second is the equally rapid escalation of technology as a way of meeting the human needs of the world's growing population, without which the human race cannot survive.
One does not hear quarrels about development in Third World countries. They want the development and will make every effort to achieve it because they know it is absolutely essential to their survival. The cost in terms of the threat of that development to the environment is not always taken into account.
It would seem that the human race is prepared to go through three stages. Hopefully we may be at the third stage. The first stage is predevelopment, which was enough to maintain a small, slowly growing population. The second, to which I have referred, is the escalation of development along with the escalation of pollution. The third stage is one to which reference has been made by other Members, and which is found not only in the Brundtland report but in the report of the National Task Force on the Environment and the Economy. It is sustained economic development, a way in which we will attempt to balance development and environmental concerns. We will attempt to balance technology and all that it provides for the human race along with safeguards against the threat which technology proposes for the human race. That is sustained economic development.
We cannot look to any simple panacea in order to provide the solution. For example, in the report of the National Task Force on the Environment and the Economy, the writers include among their recommendations this paragraph:
More research is needed on the concept of sustainable economic development and the linkages between economic development and the environment so
that we can better understand those linkages and apply data and information
to make better decisions.
I quote that paragraph for one simple reason. It shows how counterproductive it is for any of us to stand in this House and treat this problem as a simple one which could be solved simply by changing government from one party to another, changing from one ideology to another, changing from one agenda to another.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate. The motion is in the name of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). In the motion which is before the House the Hon. Member has drawn attention, and quite correctly in my view, to the fact that in Canada major economic decisions continue to be taken without incorporating into them the necessary and vital environmental safeguards that are required.
As well, the motion reminds us that the so-called Brundt-land Report, to which Canada supposedly subscribes, urges the very opposite, urges otherwise. The World Commission on Environment and Development which produced the Brundt-land report bears the official title Our Common Future. Incidentally, the Brundtland report is named after the commission's chairperson, Gro Harlem Brundtland of Norway. Interestingly enough, this report did not in any way predict ever-increasing environmental decay, poverty and hardship in an ever-polluted world among ever-decreasing resources. Not at all.
The commission does not see the world situation regarding development and the environment as being hopeless at all. That is to say it is not hopeless if there is decisive political action now, action to begin managing environmental resources to ensure both sustainable human progress on the one hand and human survival on the other.
Rather than pointing to a dark and gloomy future the commission, on the contrary, is really rather hopeful in its tone. It sees the possibility for a new era of economic growth. However, it is one that must be based on policies that, first, sustain and, second, expand the environmental resource base.
Thus I point out to the House that the Brundtland report is not at all anti-development, not at all. Rather, it believes that growth in the world economy is absolutely essential in order to relieve the great amount of poverty that is deepening in much of the developing world, sometimes referred to as the Third World.
One of the themes of the Brundtland report which is of particular or special interest to me has to do with the process of development and its effect upon indigenous or aboriginal peoples for whom the preservation of a traditional way of life in close harmony with the natural environment is essential. Brundtland points out that the gradual advance of organized development into the more remote and isolated regions of the world where many aboriginal peoples live, regions which are often rich in valuable natural resources, has the effect of

disrupting the local environment and endangering the traditional ways of life of these people.
A case in point, one rather close at hand, one that has been referred to frequently in the House of Commons, is that of the Lubicon Indian Band in the Peace River district of northern Alberta. Once a self-sufficient and proud people living in an undisturbed traditional economy they now, because of extensive resource development of oil and gas, and latterly pulp development, have been pushed aside. They have been generally excluded from any of the benefits of resource development. Consequently, they have had destroyed for them the basis of their traditional pursuits: fishing, hunting and trapping.
As a result, the Lubicon people have been reduced to a state of abject poverty. They have become welfare recipients, shack dwellers and sick. They have been stricken by an epidemic of tuberculosis which is almost unheard of anywhere else in Canada. They are depressed and hopeless.
Brundtland speaks of the increasing vulnerability of such groups left out of the processes of economic development. I quote briefly from the Commission's report which states:
Social discrimination, cultural barriers, and the exclusion of these people from national political processes makes these groups [indigenous and aboriginal people] vulnerable and subject to exploitation. Many groups become dispossessed and marginalized and their traditional practices disappear. They become the victims of what could be described as cultural extinction.
The commission goes on to describe the situation as being one of great pity, a tragedy. It is a great pity and a tragedy because these indigenous or aboriginal peoples and communities are the repositories of traditional knowledge and experience that links our humanity with its ancient origins. That is not something to which most developers ever give a passing thought. After all, resource development is a procedure engaged in primarily for profit. But Brundtland reminds us that in pursuing economic development and destroying these people there is a loss that is suffered by all of us.
Again, I quote:
Their disappearance is a loss for the larger society which could learn a great deal from their traditional skills in sustainably managing very complex ecological systems.
If we could learn that, would that not be a great step forward for humanity?
What sort of an approach or policy is needed in a nation to prevent these disasters to aboriginal and indigenous peoples from occurring? These are disasters which are directly related to the processes of resource development which no one wants to stop. I repeat again, Brundtland is not antidevelopment in its major over-all themes. What the Brundtland report calls for, interestingly enough, is a policy of self-government or selfdetermination for aboriginal peoples. Again, I quote from the report which states:
The starting point-is the recognition and protection of their traditional rights to land and other resources that sustain their way of life.

These groups [must have] their own institutions to regulate rights and obligations that are crucial for maintaining the harmony with nature and the environmental awareness characteristic of the traditional way of life.
Hence, the report goes on to say, that the "recognition of traditional rights must go hand in hand with measures to protect the local institutions that enforce responsibility in resource use. This recognition must also give local communities a decisive voice in (all matters related to) resource in the area". That is exactly, precisely what the Lubicon people in northern Alberta are asking for; it is exactly what the Nishga people in British Columbia are demanding, and there are many other instances of that kind.
By way of illustration, let me refer to the Nishga people of the northwest part of British Columbia. These people have, since time immemorial, responsibly defended, governed, managed and shared the land and the resources of the Nass River watershed.
In July, 1983, a pamphlet was published by the Nishga Tribal Council. The question was asked: "Are the Nishga people opposed to development?" They give the following answer, which I quote from the pamphlet:
We are for development. We have always seen the development of our resources as a way of enhancing our culture and traditional values. Like most concerned Canadians, we do not support the kind of development which imposes tremendous negative impacts while offering few benefits. We are for orderly, rational development which is in tune with our culture, economic interests, and long-term survival.
A period of time before this pamphlet was written the same Nishga Tribal Council did a study within the Nass River Valley on forest resources. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that we are talking now about their traditional lands, lands to which they make a very legitimate claim, lands to which they state that they have aboriginal title. This study that they undertook carefully looked at current management resources. Here is what they found.
Up to 36,000 acres of the area logged and said to be reforested is not satisfactorily reforested; 73 per cent of the best quality logged area is choked with brush; 25 per cent of the soil in logged areas has been severely damaged; high-grading has occurred, that is, the accelerated removal of the best forests; requirements for reforestation, timber utilization, forest management, planning, and protection of the environment, all of those requirements have, in many instances, been relaxed.
The answer to this type of problem, this situation, is clear. The answer is in keeping with the ethics of the Brundtland Commission, that is, a recognition of the aboriginal rights of those people, and the aboriginal title of the Nishga people. This recognition by Canada and by the Government of British Columbia ought to lead to negotiation and a satisfactory settlement of this outstanding claim.
Finally, Brundtland suggests that earnings from traditional activities can be increased through the introduction of

March 21, 1988
Supply
marketing arrangements that ensure there is a fair price for the produce from aboriginal communities. Apropos to this point, I believe a few comments would be in order concerning Canada's oldest industry, that of fur trapping. For many native people today trapping remains an essential part of life. This traditional pursuit is consistently conducted with a clear eye to conservation. Yet, trapping is coming under increasing attack from the animal rights movement which is opposed to any kind of animal use.
In the 1970s the seal industry was challenged and it was all but destroyed. The result of that was to deprive many northern Inuit communities of the main basis of their livelihood. Now the fur industry faces exactly the same threat. Recently, the British Minister of Trade indicated to the United Kingdom House of Commons that he was preparing a measure to force retailers to label some wild fur products indicating that they are derived from trapped animals. The Grand Council of the Cree said to the British Government, regarding this proposed legislation, that unlike the seal ban, not only the Inuit communities are targeted now, but aboriginal people throughout and across Canada.
Georges Erasmus, the Canadian Co-chairman of Indigenous Survival International, recently stated before a parliamentary committee that studied the fur issue that aboriginal peoples have always seen that it is possible to play a responsible productive role in nature, and it is possible for human societies to be a part of the balanced ecosystem. The animal rights group cannot accept that as a premise.
I conclude by referring again to a very important point made by the Brundtland Commission, namely, that larger societies can learn a great deal from those who practise traditional skills in sustainably managing very complex ecological systems.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate on the consideration of an opposition motion moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald):
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to act on urgent environmental issues, especially its failure to negotiate a treaty with the United States to reduce acid rain emissions; its failure to incorporate environmental matters in major economic decisions, despite endorsing the Brundtland Report and the report of the National Task Force on Environment and the Economy; and its failure to effect a clean-up of the toxic wastes contaminating the Great Lakes Basin and the St. Lawrence Seaway.
That is the motion we are debating, Mr. Speaker, and there are a great many things that could be said, beginning with acid rain. I see that the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) is present. He and I had the opportunity to serve together for some three years on the Special Committee on Acid Rain which he chaired, and as far as I know he stills chairs. It was a matter of great concern to the committee then, as I am sure it is now, that there has been no treaty on acid rain with the United States.
After all is said and done, after the summits and the Envoy's reports, and the mention of the possible negotiation of a treaty by President Reagan when he was here last year, at the end of the day we are really no further ahead with respect to actual reductions in American emissions that affect the Canadian environment.
In fact, some of us would argue that we are actually worse off because of some of the actions taken by the Conservative Government. Why are we worse off? One of the things that became clear to all committee members, whether or not they are willing to admit it, is that the Canadian Government, and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), by accepting the clean-coal technology approach of President Reagan, accepted a view of the acid rain problem which played into the hands of those on the American side who do not wish to see immediate action on acid rain.
I believe it was last June that the special committee on acid rain went to Washington. The following points were made to us over and over again by people who were our friends and allies in the States, that is to say, the people who were trying to get legislation that would actually mandate specific reductions. They said that our Prime Minister wittingly or unwittingly- that is not the point-had actually played into the hands of the very people they were fighting against, that is, the coal lobby in the United States; that it was the coal lobby that was behind the kind of approach to which the Prime Minister and the President agreed; and that we were actually making life more difficult, not less, for those whom we perceived as our allies in Congress and elsewhere in various environmental groups in the United States.
I think that is as true today as it was in June, 1987 when we were there. Nothing has come of President Reagan's last minute add-on to his speech in the House of Commons in respect of an acid rain treaty. We all know-those of us who know anything at all-that it was added as kind of a facesaving gesture so that the Prime Minister would have something to point to. I suppose that is understandable in the larger world of political images and whatnot.
However, the fact remains that if our bottom line concern, to use a phrase which I do not actually like, is whether or not there is any less acid rain falling down on Canada as a result of the policies of the Government, the conclusion must be that that is simply not the case. Maple trees continue to die in Quebec. Lakes in Ontario continue to get worse, many thousands of them to the point of being dead lakes. I would say in respect of acid rain that government policy has been a perfect failure.
As some Hon. Members will know, I was the NDP environment critic for three years. Now I am the external affairs critic and deal with things such as arms control, disarmament, regional conflicts in the Middle East and Central America, and all kinds of such things. Despite the obvious difficulty and
March 21, 1988

threat to human life and to peace in the world that these situations present, they produce much less despair in one than trying to deal with environmental issues. One thing overtook me in three years as one of the people responsible in this place for trying to bring about and to keep environmental issues on the environmental agenda when they were there. It was the fact that most of the problems about which we are talking are incremental, cumulative, and keep on doing damage to the environment every minute of every day of every week of every month that we sit here and concern ourselves with other things that I would contend are often much less important than the fact that we are persistently poisoning ourselves and the environment and putting at risk the future health of creation and of future generations. It just keeps happening. It makes one want to cry out: "Why, why can't we muster the same kind of concern about these things as can be mustered around other issues?"
A good example, as far as I am concerned, is the one on which I spoke in the House the other day in the context of a Private Member's Bill, the question of the ozone layer. We know that when styrofoam breaks down it produces or releases chlorofluorocarbons that eventually gather at a certain level in the atmosphere and break down the ozone layer. This increases the possibility of skin cancer and does other damage to the environment. Yet in one's daily life one is constantly confronted with the use of these substances, not for essential purposes. It is not as if we are talking about having to use this substance for purposes for which no other substitute can be found.
Just this morning on my way here on an Air Canada flight from Winnipeg, I noticed that all the place-mats on the plane were styrofoam. Here in the lobby of the House of Commons all the coffee cups are styrofoam. It is not just the case with Air Canada and the House of Commons. If one goes to almost any church in the country, one will be served a cup of coffee in a styrofoam cup. We are not talking about something that is essential. We are talking about something that could be easily done with something else. I flew on aircraft from Winnipeg to Ottawa for seven years without styrofoam place-mats. I never knew I missed them. There are so many things like that. We cannot even muster the collective moral will to eliminate the very small ways in which we contribute to a serious environmental problem like the erosion of the ozone layer. It seems to me that that is cause for wailing, lamenting, and gnashing of teeth. If we cannot even do those small things, how will we ever do the big things that are required and will be required whether or not we like it? It is only a question of whether we are going to wait until we are up to our necks in garbage before we do something or whether we will decide to do something today, yesterday preferably.
There was a program last night on television-and in fact there was one a couple of weeks ago-about the problem of land fill. We are running out of places to put all this stuff. It is not as if no one was saying these things 10,15, or 20 years ago. People who complained at that time about the fact that we would have to find alternatives to constantly producing non-
Supply
recyclable materials and things that go straight into the garbage were considered to be just a bunch of counter-cultural hippie nuts to which nobody should pay any attention; they were against progress. I know because I was one of those counter-cultural hippie guys who were against so-called progress. The fact remains that we were right. If many of the problems to which we pointed then had been dealt with, it would have been a whole lot easier than dealing with them now when we are at the point when we must deal with things in an emergency situation.
The City of Toronto is sitting there, not knowing what it will do next year with its garbage. It is not a very good situation. Certainly it is something that could have been prevented had there been the political will and, for that matter, the political intelligence to do so. The fact remains that there are all kinds of things that are packaged for no reason other than marketing strategies. For the sake of marketing strategies we have polluted the planet. It is because these things sell better when they are individually packaged and have a plastic this and a plastic that.
I am talking about a lot of unnecessary things that we do. It does not involve any moral dilemma; it is just the question of one generation, our generation, placing our personal, economic, material convenience higher than the well-being of future generations and higher than the well-being of creation itself.
The story the other night dealt with plastic in the oceans, with fish, marine mammals and birds literally choking to death on all the plastic that we have dumped in the oceans because it would cost too much to do something about it. Individual companies and governments, be they socialist or capitalist, it does not matter, have been guilty because they could not be bothered. It is short term efficiency. But this kind of short term efficiency has dragged us down into what will turn out to be the most inefficient thing that we ever did as a human community. Literally, in the name of these short term efficiencies, we will wipe out, if we do not smarten up, the very things which sustain us environmentally and economically. It is impossible to talk about a healthy economy without talking and acting at the same time about having a sustainable environment. That was one of the points made over and over again by the Brundtland report.
Over the years we have externalized environmental costs or they have not been paid at all, they have just been lying there waiting to be paid. Things like clean air, clean water, fertile soil and naturally occurring forests and everything else have not been figured into the cost of doing business, into the cost of our economic way of life. So whoever happened to get there first, whoever happened to get to the clean air, the clean water or the naturally occurring forest first and got the rights from the Crown or whatever the case may be would do just whatever liked. That may have worked for 50, 60 or 70 years, the very short time that we have just done what we pleased with

March 21, 1988
Supply
our air, soil, water and forests. It will turn out to be historically a very short period of time but a very historically significant time if we do not change our ways. The people of the future will look back and say: "Would you believe those guys in the 20th century?" Would you believe what they did between 1910 and 1990?" Or whatever the period may be. "Would you believe the incredible lack of foresight or the incredible moral responsibility of what they did in a period of 80 to 90 years to that which took thousands and thousands of years to build up?" Woe I say to the generation that is able to be accused of that. Yet that is exactly the kind of accusation which can be made against the people of the 20th century. We can only hope that in the latter days of this century we will smarten up and do everything that is in our power to do in order to rectify the very terrible situation in which we have got ourselves.
There have been a few victories, I suppose, Mr. Speaker. They should not go unmentioned. The resolution of the problem with respect to South Moresby is the one little victory and a significant one that comes to mind. But people are still camped out at Strathcona Park on Vancouver Island trying to protect one of the oldest provincial parks in British Columbia from the kind of mining exploration which the provincial Government has decided to permit. The battle goes on.
The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) mentioned something on which I hope I still have some time to comment, namely, the whole question of the fur lobby and that in the past a very successful campaign was waged against the seal hunt. That campaign has now been extended by animal rights groups and others to all fur products, and the appropriate cabinet Minister in the British Government is considering some kind of action which would discourage people from purchasing Canadian fur products.
I want to put on the record my opposition to this kind of action by the animal rights groups and by the British Government, if it chooses to take this kind of action.
To the extent that the environmental movement has been involved in this, although some groups like Greenpeace appear to be pulling back from their activity and participation in the anti-fur lobby, they have participated in something which has undermined the economic viability and the traditional lifestyles of people who are their natural allies. It seems to me that the native people and environmentalists are in many ways natural allies. I have always regretted the extent to which some in the environmental community have participated in the antifur lobby. I am glad to see that many in the environmental movement are coming to perceive that this is an inappropriate course of action for them. One of the things I think is important to the over-all sustainability of the environment is the sustainability of native lifestyles and native communities.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, you were signalling that I have little time left, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is nodding in agreement. With that, I will bring my remarks to a close.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) for his contribution to this debate. In particular I paid attention to the part where he referred to his plane trip this morning and the styrofoam cups that we use here in the House. I decided to make a quick inquiry about his comment on the cups to see whether the Member was right, but I do not know the answer. This is the kind of problem consumers have. Members of Parliament are supposed to be particularly well informed about issues of this nature. As I said, I made some quick inquiries and was told that styrofoam cups are okay, that CFCs are not used as an agent for blowing in making these cups. Instead they use hydrocarbons such as propane or butane. While I asked my interlocutor how can one identify what cups have CFCs and which do not, I was told that cups which break up into little chunks and bubbles when you pick away at them are okay, that CFCs are not involved in them. Apparently the ones that use CFCs are smooth. I have part of a cup here that we use in the lobby. I started to rip it apart. If they rip like paper, apparently they are supposed to contain CFCs. I suppose you can guess, Mr. Speaker, that I am somewhat confused in that it is difficult to determine what kind of cups contain CFCs and what kind of cups do not.
This reminds me of a point I made when speaking in a debate on the environment several weeks ago. I said that one of the things the Government could do, even if it did not want to ban outright the use of CFCs, would be to require that products containing CFCs be labelled as such, allowing consumers to make intelligent decisions about whether they want to purchase such products or not. It is a point I felt that I would like to raise in this debate, and I invite the Hon. Member to respond if he would care to.

Mr. Speaker, there are kinds of foam that do not contain CFCs, and part of the problem, as the Hon. Member has said so well, is that one is not always aware what foam is which. The idea of labelling is certainly a good half measure but the best thing would be not to permit these products to be made in the first place, particularly if there are alternatives, and there are. However, even if hydrocarbon or something else is used as a blowing agent rather than CFCs, there is still the secondary environmental problem which is that these are non-biodegradable substances. In fairness, though, that is not what I was talking about when I was speaking.
The Hon. Member made a good point. Just recently in my home province, the Government announced an aid package for a company that was making styrofoam egg cartons. If those styrofoam egg cartons are being made with the kind of foam that contains CFCs, then this is hardly an instance of integrating environmental and economic decisions. I cannot say for sure exactly what process will be used-

They're going to use the good stuff.
March 21, 1988
I am told by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) that it was the good stuff, not the stuff with CFCs.
But it wasn't cardboard either.

In any event, at least it was not CFCs. Had it been, that would have been a classic example of economic and environmental decisions being at odds with each other. The fact that the process does not use CFCs is certainly something I am glad to hear. I see that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood checked that out.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to add some input into what I think is an extremely timely and very important motion which is before the House today. The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) and members of her Party have been constantly supporting issues that relate to the environment.
Someone said to me the other weekend that we should start treating Canada as if we planned to stay here for a while. Indeed, we do. As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) just mentioned, those who come after us will look back and ask why we did this, why we did that and why we were so concerned about resource exploitation. They will ask why the Government of the day was not focusing more aggressively on issues of immediate impact on the environment.
The environment knows no partisan politics. I invite all Hon. Members to bone up on environmental issues because I think it will be a major point of confrontation during the next election campaign. If Members or candidates are not conscious of the environment in their own neighbourhoods, provinces and country, they will be facing pretty tough questions from their constituents or their potential constituents.
I want to speak briefly today on securing sustainable development in Canada with the following points of view. I want to talk about the Government's record on implementing the principles of sustaining development as described in the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development and Canada's national task force on environment and the economy.
Almost a year ago, the world commission, commonly known as the Brundtland Commission, released its landmark document entitled Our Common Future. Canada called for this commission and Canada generously supported and funded it throughout all of its work. We commend those who produced the final report.
In the broad sense, the Brundtland report is not one of despair. Rather, it is a message of hope. Simply stated, the commission argued that every nation must integrate environmental considerations into economic decisions. Our Common Future envisions a new era of growth through sustainable development.
Supply
In his speech to the United Nations last fall, our Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said the following to the assembly:
The environment and economy cannot be addressed as two separate global problems; only by viewing the two as one can either be resolved.
The federal Minister of the Environment went on to say at the assembly in his recommendations that the concept of sustainable development should be supported and that UN agencies and affiliates should ensure that their programs reflect that concept.
Canada worked very hard within the assembly to ensure unanimous support for a resolution passed last December calling upon all Governments, the United Nations and multilateral and development institutions to review and ensure that their policies and programs contribute directly to sustainable development. Canada has already been successful in having the food and agricultural organization and the UN industrial development organization adopt a resolution on the concept of sustainable development.
As Hon. Members know, at the Commonwealth heads of Government meeting in Vancouver last year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), along with all of the other Commonwealth leaders, agreed that the goal of environmentally sustainable development should be central to national and international economic policy. As we have seen recently, an announcement was made a few weeks ago indicating that CIDA, our Canadian aid program, will try to do everything it can to concentrate aid on projects that would ensure that sustainable development is realized in countries throughout the world to which we give assistance.
Hon. Members might recall that years ago, I lived and worked in eastern, central and southern Africa in the areas of national parks, wildlife and tourism. Aside from having a remarkable learning experience, I was impressed by the fact that the Tanzanians, Kenyans, Zimbabweans and Malawians recognize that within the context of their own environmental development, their wildlife resources and national parks play a very important part in sustaining the future of their countries.
I recently returned there, just three months ago, after being away for 11 years. Although these countries face great hardships, their leaders, Ministers and Members of Parliament with whom I met continue to underline the value of the land and the value of their natural resources to the sustainable growth within their own countries. Let us recall that these are very, very poor countries. It would be easy for them to just brush that aside and develop the land, cut down all the trees and kill all the wildlife. These people live from day to day and from week to week, but they have recognized the importance of maintaining sustainable growth in their own countries.
Last September, Canada hosted a diplomatic conference at which 22 countries signed what is now called the Montreal Protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer. Canada s effort will continue to focus on the management of the global commons in the atmospheric sector, mainly through support

March 21, 1988
Supply
for the development of a law of the air. Canadians are also deeply concerned about global climate change, and Canada will host an international conference in June in Toronto that will address the issue among other atmospheric issues. The conference is called "The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security" and is another example of Canada's commitment to the Brundtland Commission's call for prudent management of the global commons.
I want to talk a bit about something that has been very important to the over-all context of the environment and important to me and to the people of Ottawa-Carleton. The international co-operation to secure an abundance of wildlife as recommended by the Brundtland Commission is already evident through co-operation between Canada and its neighbour, the United States. In 1986, Canada and the U.S. signed a $ 1.5-billion North American waterfowl management plan to restore and enhance waterfowl populations.
The plan, which is a milestone in multilevel government and private-sector co-operation, aims principally at conserving habitat beneficial to both wildlife and agricultural interests. I underline that it is of benefit to both wildlife and agricultural interests. It will be of extreme importance in western Canada, the breeding grounds of the North American waterfowl. Once this plan is fully implemented, enhanced water-fowl populations will make a valuable economic contribution to all regions of North America.
We have heard reference to acid rain here today. We all know how serious that problem is. The Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) has been leading the charge for many years to get not only his Government and our country to recognize the importance of this transboundary problem, but to get the Americans to recognize its importance as well. Last year at a conference in Quebec City a report was released by a man named Paul Hansen from the Izaak Walton League of America. It is called Acid Rain and Water-Fowl: The Case for Concern in North America. In the forward to the report he refers to this devastating problem and I quote:
Now comes this report from Paul W. Hansen of the Izaak Walton League of America, pointing to the involvement of acid rain in the welfare of breeding ducks. Based upon preliminary research by Canadian and U.S. biologists, this report presents sobering information on the adverse effects of acid rain on Black Duck and other duck populations.
In North America, particularly eastern North America, since 1955 the Black Duck population has declined by 60 per cent. This beautiful bird used to be called the Crown Prince of the Atlantic Flyway. It has been conclusively proven by these researchers that acid rain is having a very negative impact on the breeding habits and habitats of the Black Duck. That is a barometer which says we have to act and act quickly. When you see that kind of a reduction in the number of water-fowl, you know we have a serious environmental problem.
World Wildlife Fund Canada has been working aggressively in co-operation with the federal Government, provincial
Governments and the private sector in many important areas of wildlife habitat and restoration. In fact, they are working on what is called the Canadian Endangered Species Program. Last year the federal Government announced a new program within the context of the Endangered Species Recovery Fund involving $1 million over the next four years. Let me just quote a word or two from the last annual report of the fund concerning this work:
In 1986, a rather sad Canadian milestone was reached. The national list compiled by the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada officially exceeded 100 species.
That should not be happening. For whatever reason, 86 per cent of all Canadians have expressed the view that saving endangered species is important to them. The federal Government made a commitment to spend $1 million to assist with these programs. Whether it be the Bald Eagle, the bison in Wood Buffalo National Park, or other endangered species, many projects are being pursued and we are going to continue to co-operate in an effort to enhance the potential of our wildlife resources throughout the country.
The World Wildlife Fund Canada is also involved in administering the Wildlife Toxicology Fund which is fully funded by the federal Government. They submitted a report to the Minister of the Environment last April. Monte Hummel, the Executive Co-ordinator of the fund, concludes, based on this federal support, and I quote again:
The first 19 months of operation of the Wildlife Toxicology Fund have been immensely successful by any measurement. The quality and diversity of work supported is second to none, and we have achieved the desired leverage effect of using Environment Canada funding to secure financial support from others.
An excellent example of co-operation between federal funds and the private sector administered through a third party organization, the very well-known and successful World Wildlife Fund for Canada. I congratulate Mr. Hummel and all of his colleagues for their efforts and we look forward to expanding those efforts.
The Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers put together a national task force on the environment in the economy. The Prime Minister and all provincial Premiers discussed and endorsed the report of that task force at the conference of First Ministers last November. The Prime Minister stated that we must encourage economic growth in harmony with our environment. That addresses very clearly and concisely the concerns brought forward by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood in her motion which we are now debating.
As was recently referred to by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill we had a significant achievement last year with the magnificent archipelago off the West Coast of British Columbia known as South Moresby. The islands contain some of the last virgin rain forest in Canada. It contains many unique plant and animal species. These islands are also home of the Haida Nation, a nation rich in cultural heritage. The economic value of the timber contained in the rain forest on the islands created for Governments and the
March 21, 1988

forest industry a difficult trade-off between short-term and long-term interests, and between regional and national values.
Through co-operative efforts of Government, industry and the people of South Moresby, environmental and economic goals were finally reconciled and a national park will soon be created there as part of a multimillion dollar economic development strategy for the area. This is based on the sustainable development concept which ties directly into the discussion we are having today in reference to the Brundtland Commission report. The Haida's role in the strategy will be central. Canada will be working to develop similar demonstrations of how environmental and economic considerations can be successfully integrated through this kind of partnership and co-operation.
Reference has also been made to energy and how it relates to not only Canada's use, needs, future and present, but also within the context of the free trade agreement. The Hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) should be congratulated for his success in applying the Brundtland message in his area of responsibility. The department has an impressive action plan to integrate environment and economy which addresses the inclusion of environmental considerations in cabinet documents and the rigorous application of environmental assessment. This approach can be considered as a progressive model for government departments at all levels. Indeed, the federal agenda calls for the integration of environmental considerations into the policies of all federal departments.
Within the context of sustainable development, to meet this challenge as well in the agriculture sector, for example, federal and provincial Governments have collaborated in developing a national agriculture strategy. This strategy acknowledges that soil and water resources must be protected and improved through conservation and development programs, thereby guaranteeing agricultural productivity for future generations.
We have also seen a national policy for managing fish habitat instituted pursuant to the federal Fisheries Act. Its long-term objective is an over-all net increase in the productive capacity of fish habitat, to be achieved through conservation, restoration, and the development of habitat for aquatic plants, fish, shellfish, crustaceans, and marine animals in general.
Recently, the federal Government announced a new national water policy. I am pleased that it has done so, as I am sure you are, Mr. Speaker, The water in the Hamilton area is not exactly drinkable.
Witnesses recently appeared before the legislative committee studying the environmental protection legislation. They were extremely concerned about the pollutants, chemicals, waste and toxins that are not only killing the Niagara River but the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence. Canada used to be
Supply
known as a country with beautiful lakes, rivers and wildlife. These are finite resources and can only withstand a certain amount of punishment. They have been punished for decades.
We must recognize that in order to achieve sustainable economic growth there must be an environmental component to every project we undertake, whether it is a housing project, a mining project, a forestry project, the creation of a national park or the utilization of our rivers for hydroelectricity.
We must never lose sight of the importance of the environment. The national water policy is very timely. The Rideau River flows through the City of Ottawa and empties into the Ottawa River. When I was young, I used to swim in the Rideau River at an area known as Mooney's Bay.
Today, at best there are 40 days during the summer when one can go in the water. I will be asking the federal Government to work closely with the Province of Ontario, the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and the Cities of Ottawa and Nepean to clean up Mooney's Bay under its national water policy. They will spend a lot of money this year through Parks Canada, the National Capital Commission and the Regional Municipality of Ottawa Carleton to develop a marina at Mooney's Bay which is sorely needed. Today, anyone who falls into Mooney's Bay may have to be rushed to the Riverside Hospital for a tetanus shot. We need to enhance the tertiary treatment to our storm sewage drainage system. In that context the Brundtland Report even touches the Rideau River.
The Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka is well aware of the importance of the tourism industry in his riding. It is absolutely essential. Tourism is vital in all of Canada. It is the second largest employer in the National Capital Region.
If we do not enhance the quality of our lakes and rivers, we will face serious consequences in the future. Last spring I had the privilege of visiting for the first time a northern part of Canada. I spent a week at Tuktoyaktuk and had an opportunity to visit Holman and Victoria Islands. Although the North is magnificent and quite beautiful, where I experienced 24 hours of daylight for the first time, what I saw were barrels, drums, oil spills, garbage, boards, piles of steel and used fencing lying everywhere. That was not my vision of the North.
I spoke to the Minister responsible for natural resources in the North and talked to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), and to the Minister of the Environment. I said it is necessary to work together because places like Tuktoyaktuk will not sustain themselves if we do not protect the fragile environment.
This is a very important motion before the House today and all Members should take heed. If our environment dies, we will die with it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, take a few moments to speak in this debate on the environment, the subject raised in an Opposition motion presented here in the House.
It is perfectly true that the people of my province, that Quebecers are very concerned about the quality of the environment, and I would say that concern is increasing.
I realize that Canadians on the whole are becoming increasingly concerned about the environment, but last month, the results of a public opinion poll conducted by the firm Leger et Leger in Quebec, showed that Quebecers are even more concerned about the environment then we thought. I will mention some of the facts discovered by this well-known polling firm which published the results of the survey in the Journal de Montreal of February 10. People are now very much concerned about the quality of the environment in Quebec, as much as 83 per cent. We can say this has now become a major political issue.
People were asked: Generally speaking, what kind of pollution do you think is most harmful? Of the persons
surveyed, 33 per cent mentioned acid rain; 28.8 per cent thought all forms of pollution were harmful, and I think they are right; 19.5 per cent thought air pollution was most harmful, while 13 per cent mentioned water pollution. When people were asked what they thought was mainly responsible for pollution, 70 per cent put industry first. One of the most important and surprising discoveries was how people answered the following question: Would you be in favour of separating your garbage into waste paper, plastic and glass, for recycling purposes? Seventy-seven per cent of respondents said yes.
This demonstrates that people are not only concerned about the environment but are also prepared to make an effort to clean up their surroundings. They are prepared to go even further, as we see in the answer to the following question: Would you be willing to pay a special anti-pollution tax to improve the quality of the environment? Usually when taxpayers are asked whether they want to pay an additional tax, the answer is no. In this case, 59.3 per cent said yes, they were willing to pay a special tax to fight pollution.
Finally, I think the House would also be interested in the answer to another question. People were asked: Do you think environmental regulations in Quebec are strict enough or not strict enough? Not strict enough, said 83 per cent.
That is how important the quality of the environment and cleaning up the environment has become to our Quebec constituents. It is not surprising, because the headlines in the media are increasingly bringing major problems to our attention. For instance, here is one headline, and I have several that go back one or two years.
In La Presse of February 26, 1987: Le Quebec est devenu la fosse septique des Grands Lacs (Quebec, the Great Lakes' Septic Tank). No wonder people were getting concerned when more recently, in November 1987, Le Devoir mentioned the renewal of the Great Lakes water quality agreement between Canada and the United States, it pointed out that the St. Lawrence was not included. The St. Lawrence was not included as part of the Great Lakes system, although all environmental experts had recommended this long ago.
Here is a headline from March 5, 1987. That was a year ago, but I will get back to this one because "a year later, we still have the same situation". Here we have a headline showing a photograph of the Minister of Environment (Mr. McMillan), who said on the subject of cleaning up Quebec's waterways that: "Ottawa won't spend a cent".
According to one study, Quebec is the province most severely threatened by acid rain. No wonder Quebecers are becoming increasingly concerned about environmental issues. This study was released and discussed at the end of an international forum on acid rain held in Montreal. This was in February, which means last month. "The federal Minister of the Environment", said the article, "refused to take part in this seminar organized by I'Union des producteurs agricoles (UPA). Officially, the Minister had declined", the article read, "because he had to accept an award from the Governor
March 21, 1988

General in Toronto. However, it was rumoured in UPA circles that the Union's opposition to free trade had caused a breakdown in relations between the UPA and the Minister of the Environment". The result was, of course, that the Minister failed to participate in an important conference on acid rain.
Meanwhile, the Quebec Minister of the Environment was doing his best to go it alone.
Here we read: "Lincoln will set up an action committee to clean up the St. Lawrence". Lincoln was of course prepared to spend a lot of money, but he expected the federal Government to do its share. A year ago in June 1987, we read: "Lincoln is sure Quebec will get $ 100 million from Ottawa to clean up the St. Lawrence River."
In a few minutes I will tell you what Lincoln said on a television broadcast exactly six days ago. He was still negotiating to get his $100 million.
I have here a cartoon that appeared in Le Devoir on February 19, 1988. We are not supposed to show pictures here in the House so I will describe it. It shows a huge grey cloud drawn to represent the American flag, with stars and stripes in dark and light grey. We see drops falling on a forest which are actually miniature missiles, piercing maple leaves. This picture reflects the message Quebec's farmers, through their union, I'Union des producteurs agricoles, have tried to get through to the federal Government several times. In January 1987, the UPA wrote to the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark) at the House of Commons, commenting on the report of the Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry.
Quoting statistics, the UPA said that if we compared the number of maple taps in 1986 to the number of taps in the eight, previous years, already 2 million taps had been lost during that time, largely due to acid rain. This is important when we realize that, in Quebec, usually 14 million trees are tapped annually. This means one-seventh has already been lost.
The UPA, very direct in its strategy unlike any other movement in this country, presented the federal Government with a bill for the loss in revenue suffered by farmers. It did so because the federal Government had so far failed to do enough, especially in the area of research. If we compare the work done in this area to what the federal Government has done, says the UPA, the Government's efforts are not only insufficient but laughable, unless we consider that a total of $30,000 spent in 1986 on research on the impact of acid rain on maple trees is worth mentioning.
According to the UPA, the Government of Quebec was practically bearing the total cost of research on the decline of maple stands and deciduous forests, a forecast $1 million for that year.
It was then the UPA decided to take the unusual step of sending a bill to the federal Government. However, six months later the Minister of the Environment said before a Committee of the House that he never heard about it. At this point I

would like to quote from a letter that Bernard Duval, first vice-president of the UPA, wrote to the Minister of the Environment, in which he said: "We were astonished at what you said". In answer to a question from Mr. Penner, a Liberal Member who was on the Committee during the hearings of the Special Committee on Acid Rain, the Minister said on December 2: "Mr. Chairman, I must confess I am not aware of any overture made by the industry directly to the Government for assistance. I am unaware of the application from the industry for assistance from the federal Government to compensate, or to make up for the decrease of productivity." However, six months before, in a letter to the Prime Minister and to Mr. Merrithew (Minister of State (Forestry and Mines)), the UPA wrote, and I quote: "-sent a bill for $87 million, for losses incurred by maple producers." This goes to show what the UPA is up against when it tries to deal with the very serious problems they are facing in Quebec.
Nevertheless, I must give the Minister of the Environment some credit on acid rain. Granted, the Minister was unable to make the United States realize that we must be prepared to spend money on fighting acid rain, but he may have been able to make the U.S. acknowledge the fact that acid rain can cause damage. The Minister has managed to conclude agreements between the federal Government and the provinces under which, here in Canada, we are committed to reducing S02 by 50 per cent between now and 1994. However, the Minister is having trouble convincing the Americans to set similar standards for emission reduction. If the Minister is to be credited for concluding certain agreements with the provinces, I think we should also give credit to the previous Minister, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), who started negotiations with the provinces in 1984 before the present Government came to power.
I am willing, therefore, to give some credit to the current Minister, but I suggest I should also give some credit to the previous Minister who had initiated the process of nitrogen oxyde reductions by adopting regulations which were finally implemented in late 1984. These regulations make it compulsory to use catalytic converters to reduce the level of nitrogen oxydes in the atmosphere. These devices are standard equipment on all 1988 new car models sold in Canada.
In 1983, the Hon. Member for Davenport was already doing his share by starting the progressive removal of leaded gas. This type of gas is still sold, but less and less, and modern vehicules now use unleaded gas, which is advantageous.
I would like to remind the House that the last two provinces-New Brunswick and Nova Scotia-have just signed these emission limitation agreements.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the cleaning of the St. Lawrence river, a river which is very important not only for navigation, but also because a very large portion of the Quebec population lives on its shores. Metropolitan Montreal, with nearly one third of the Quebec population, is surrounded by the St. Lawrence River. I remember with melancoly the time

when, as a young boy, I used to swim in the St. Lawrence when it was still possible to do so. Needless to say, Montrealers have been deprived of this pleasure for many years, but we hope, because of the efforts made by the Hon. Clifford Lincoln, our own Quebec Minister of the Environment, to see the day when it will be possible again to go for a swim in the St. Lawrence River.
Minister Lincoln has announced a $3 billion investment project over a 10 year period which could clean up the St. Lawrence river by 80 per cent. At the same time, it is seeking from Ottawa a meagre contribution of $100 million over the next five years which he has not been able to obtain so far, unless, unknown to me, he obtained it in an agreement signed last night.
I have here a written transcript of the Mid-day program of March 15, 1988-six days ago

during which the Hon. Cliff Lincoln explained his $3 billion clean-up and investment project. He was asked:

"How much are you getting from Ottawa?" Was is the question. The answer was, "Well, we are not yet getting money. We are just talking to Ottawa right now. We are talking to Ottawa for a $100 million contribution over five years".

So that is what Minister Lincoln was doing or had begun doing a year ago. There is no reason to say that the Minister of the Environment has been overzealous when it comes to cleaning up the St. Lawrence River.
And what most irks Montrealers, Mr. Speaker, is that when this Minister of the Environment comes to Montreal he does so to brag about his accomplishments. I recall that during one such visit about a year ago he practically insulted Montrealers by telling them that, as he saw it, the St. Lawrence River was so polluted that it looked like an open sewer. I agree with the Minister that the St. Lawrewnce is like an open sewer in the Montreal region. But as Montrealers, what is the percentage in listening to the Minister telling us that our river is dirty if he has to be coaxed to make a much smaller contribution than the amount the Government of Quebec is prepared to put up. In fact, if the Quebec Government is ready to put up $3 billion over ten years, this works out to $300 milion a year. They are asking Ottawa for $ 100 million over five years, or $20 million a year.
That is much less, like fifteen times less. So I would suggest to the Minister of the Environment that if he should come back to Montreal he might indeed make resounding pronouncements if he is so inclined, but I wish he would also bring his wallet and tell us how much money he is prepared to spend to clean up our river-the wish of all Montrealers-instead of always cutting the funds earmarked for the environment, down 17 per cent as they are now when compared with what was available in 1984 when the Conservatives took over.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because it is a subject about which I have always felt very strongly. I grew up in the Prairies of western Canada and spent a great deal of time in British Columbia and Central Canada. I have watched and was one like all the rest of us who was guilty of the ruining of our environment, the polluting of our air and water, and the degradation of our lands and forests.
I am not rising to point a finger of blame at any one person, any one Party or any one Government concerning the state of our environment and our ecology. I point a finger of blame at all Governments at all levels for failing to act. That includes Governments of all Parties. I point a finger of blame at these Governments for failing to act sufficiently.
"By their deeds shall you know them". The deeds of us all as individuals, of Governments at all levels as well as corporations, farm organizations and unions are all guilty of failure. The point is that from this day on what will we do about it?
It will cost money. It will cost a great deal of money. It will cost profits. It will cost a great deal of profits. However, if we really mean what we say, and I have listened to Members from all sides of the House today, then we must be prepared to pay those costs.
I said that I would not point fingers. I do not cite the following figures just at the Conservative Government of today. I cite them only as an example of what previous Governments have done in Ottawa, as well as what previous Governments have done in the provinces. They are only meant as an example. I hope the Government and all other Governments of all other Parties at all other levels have learned some lessons from these figures.
I believe that all political Parties have made excellent policy statements on the environment. I believe that they mean what they say in those statements. Let us learn a lesson from what the Government did by, let us say, inadvertence, because the concern over the deficit took priority over the concern of the welfare and the priorities of the environment.
In the fall of 1984 when the ink was hardly dry on the ballots, $33.6 million was cut from the Department of the Environment, which wiped out 416 positions. Many of those positions were held by internationally known and recognized researchers. The Canadian Wildlife Service was cut by 23 per cent. A research program monitoring toxic pollution of the Great Lakes, which led to the initial identification of dioxin contamination, was eliminated. I have listened to several speakers today complain about the toxin levels in the Great Lakes. The darn program was eliminated in the fall of 1984.
The Wildlife Interpretation Centres were closed. National park expansion and improvement programs were slashed by just about $20 million. Support for the Toxicology Research Centre in Ontario was withdrawn. In a related move, the environmental secretariat at the National Research Council
March 21, 1988

was closed. The centre employed 17 scientists and support staff. It was conducting important studies, including the effect of lead poisoning on young children. If something is going to be done about lead poisoning, there must be research. Well, Mr. Speaker, it was closed.
I started off by saying that this is going to cost money. Anyone who does not recognize that fact does not intend to do anything about it. It is going to cost money even if it means an increase in the deficit. It is the type of increase that is not an expense but an investment in the future of this nation and in the future of our environment.
I put the question to my colleagues in this House, I put it to every citizen in Canada of this present generation, my generation, the generation of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) who is a generation after me, and to the generation of my hon. friend from Bow River, who is the generation ahead of me-actually he looks younger than I am. There are three generations of Members in this Chamber and I put the question to all of us: Who do we think we are? We have no right, not even a privilege to leave the type of mess that our children will inherit a lot of already, and our grandchildren and great grandchildren will inherit. We have no right to leave that. We have no right to pass on all of those costs of cleaning up our environment to those generations. We must put hundreds of millions of dollars a year starting this year, now, into cleaning up the mess that we have left.
It seems to me that Governments of all political stripes have been influenced too much by what I call the industrial and economic development syndrome which, if there is a buck to be made, that takes priority. The evidence is there for anyone to peruse; "anything to make a buck". It means misusing our forests, our water, and our air, but if we can get another plant, another industry, some more jobs, we will do it. Any one of us can throw out facts and figures in the House of Commons about how many more jobs have been created without looking at what has been done to our air, our water, our land, and our forests in the meantime.
It seems to me that those who would put development ahead of anything else are the ones, in my opinion, who would dig a mine over their mother's grave, if they thought they could make a buck. They are the ones who would deplete our forests, ruin our air or ruin our water if it made for a good bottom line on the annual report and the dividends to the shareholders, no matter what harm they had caused for succeeding generations and the costs that succeeding generations would have to pay.
In my opinion, the person who is operating a mine, or operating a forest industry, should be required by law to put as much or more back into the environment as they took out. They have to be required to do so by law, otherwise they should not be allowed to operate. There are a number of countries in western Europe where that has been done for

years, and they are of various political stripes. I know that that flies in the face of the U.S.A. version of what North America should be, that it should be wide open for the entrepreneur, and the bottom line profit syndrome. But I do not think, in fact I am convinced, that the overwhelming majority of Canadians do not want that type of attitude in this country. Of course, it is an international problem. That is no excuse for us not doing what we should and can do in cleaning up our own mess within the territorial boundaries of Canada.
What about our water, for example all the very modest programs that we used to have on sewage treatment, and for the last number of years it has been impossible to receive any type of federal assistance for the treatment of sewage. Yet, there are still metropolitan areas in Canada that pour raw sewage into the rivers. Under the Constitution that is a violation of what is in the best interest of the nation as a whole. Ottawa could say to the municipalities, the metropolitan areas, and the provinces that are allowing this to happen, "If you do not stop it, we will step in and stop it for you and you will pay your share". That has to do with what I believe the Constitution calls the good order and the good works for the benefit of Canada. What is done that is deleterious and deteriorating to the people along the St. Lawrence River or the Great Lakes harms not only those people, but harms the whole nation.
I would say to those who are harvesting our forests that it must be treated like a harvest and in no other way. For every tree they cut, they must plant two or three more, because some of them will not survive. That has to be a cost of their doing business. It should not be necessary to give them some kind of a tax benefit for reforestation. If they cut the tree down, they must plant at least two in its place. If they are not prepared to do that, they should then be asked to leave and we will let someone in who will do that. No one should have to receive a tax benefit for leaving the environment the way they found it, no matter what enterprise they are involved in.
I would say the same thing about land use on the Prairies, where I come from. We keep misusing land and farming land that should never have been farmed. Some of it should be returned to grass and prairie. Some of it should be replanted to trees that were cut down by our fathers and grandfathers.
We should be required to use good tillage practices so that the top few inches of prairie soil is not turned into something that looks like flour which, when the wind blows and it does not rain, moves about in the air and drifts into the ditches.
A moment ago I talked about water. Technology has been in place for years, a tertiary sewage treatment system, whereby we can convert common, ordinary sewage into water which is almost drinkable. I see my good friend opposite smiling, but he knows that I am right; it is almost drinkable. However, we can return it to the environment at a point where it will not cause any further harm to the waters which receive that treated sewage. Technology is also in place to use semi-treated sewage
