as a fertilizer or left where it is. I know that that does not make fertilizer or chemical companies very happy, but that is too bad.
I do not think there is any point in the Government continuing to consider the Department of the Environment as a minor or junior department. The fact of the matter is that it is a major department which needs to be treated as such. It needs the funding which it deserves. Whether the Conservatives, the Liberals, or the New Democrats are in power, any one of the three Parties that does not do so deserves the condemnation of the entire population of Canada. We need the political will to do it.
I close by repeating what I said earlier. Who do we think we are that we can leave the kind of mess that the present generation is creating to future generations to pay for? We caused it. We should pay for it. We should clean it up.

Mr. Speaker, I am more than pleased to enter into the debate today. I commend the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) for bringing this matter forth on an opposition day.
Needless to say, I feel that the Government has achieved a great deal. However, I am also well aware that there is more we can achieve and more we must do.
Let me begin by agreeing that indeed acid rain is a very serious threat to the environment, especially to the economy of the country including the economy of Ontario, the industrial heartland. Quite literally the facts speak for themselves.
More than 350,000 lakes in eastern Canada are vulnerable. Tens of thousands of them have lost 60 per cent to 80 per cent of their neutralizing capacity. Approximately 150,000 lakes have a PH level of less than 6.0, the acidity level at which detrimental effects begin to occur. Some 14,000 lakes have already been acidified. This means that they have a PH level of less than 5.0 and are essentially devoid of normal aquatic life.
I am well aware that the figures are pretty large when it comes to lakes. However, Ontario and Quebec are indeed very fortunate. It is estimated that Ontario has 800,000 lakes, more or less, and that Quebec has in excess of one million. More than 50 per cent of eastern Canada's forests grow in areas where rainfall is acidic. More than 80 per cent of all Canadians live in areas where acidic deposits exceed acceptable levels.
As if this litany of environmental concerns were not enough, economically acid rain is endangering the natural resource base in an area of eastern Canada which measures about 2.6 million square kilometres. This resource base sustains approximately 8 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product and some 255,000 jobs.
I am proud to remind the House that the Government has tackled this threat to the Canadian environment and economy head on. In March, 1985, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the implementation of a comprehensive national
acid rain abatement program which will slash Canadian sulphur dioxide emissions by 50 per cent of 1980 allowable levels by 1994 at the latest.
Essentially the Canadian abatement program was designed to address three objectives. First, Canadian emission reductions will reduce the damage we are causing to ourselves. Second, the Prime Minister recognized that Canada must have clean hands if we expect the United States to take action. Third, Canada has a responsibility to reduce the damage to which it is contributing in the northeastern United States.
The federal Government has set a clear and straightforward yardstick against which to measure progress on the acid rain issue. We have determined that acid fall-out must be reduced to less than 20 kilograms per hectare in all vulnerable areas. Our scientists have found that damage occurs when acid rain fall-out is above this amount. I am pleased to say that they have also found evidence that when acid fall-out drops below this threshold number, recovery of the environment starts to take place.
Calculations have been done which tell us how many tonnes and where sulphur dioxide emissions must be cut to achieve the 20 kilograms per hectare per year objective. We have concluded that total annual sulphur dioxide emissions from the Saskatchewan-Manitoba border eastward must be reduced to 2.3 million tonnes, and that the transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide into eastern Canada must be reduced to about 2 million tonnes.
The federal Government has shown great leadership in developing Canada's part of the bargain. As a measure of the Government's ability to work constructively with provincial counterparts, all seven federal-provincial agreements required to implement the Canadian acid rain abatement program have been signed.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is certainly to be commended in this regard. Some of them had to be hauled in, almost kicking and screaming, before we got their signatures on the line. All these agreements specified that the required reductions will be achieved by 1994 at the latest.
Current sulphur dioxide emissions in eastern Canada are about 2.8 million tonnes, 35 per cent less than they were in 1980. This illustrates that Canada is well on its way to achieving the necessary reductions in its sulphur dioxide emissions. We can all be proud of our abatement program. We will all benefit from the results.
The federal Government has also put into place strong nitrogen oxide emission controls. Cars and trucks account for about 40 per cent of total Canadian NOx emissions. As of September 1, 1987, all new cars and light trucks sold in Canada were required to meet the most stringent emission standards, requiring the use of the state of the art control technology. The standards for heavy duty trucks take effect
March 21, 1988

December 1, 1988 which is, in fact, nine months sooner than in the United States. These will reduce NOx emissions from mobile sources in Canada by up to 45 per cent by the year 2000. I will admit, Mr. Speaker, that I was one of those who was pushing the Government very hard in 1985 to see if at all possible those controls could be applied on the 1987 model cars, but I was not successful. However, in 1988 we will. As the Minister remarked in his comments this morning, leaded gasoline will be outlawed by 1992. That will also certainly help the NOx emissions.
Once fully implemented, the Canadian Acid Rain Abatement Program is estimated to cost the private sector and provincial utilities about $500 million annually. This comes on top of our comprehensive local ambient air quality program. I believe a similar figure for the United States is about $5 billion a year. As my hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), said pollution control is pretty expensive. It certainly does not come easy. Canada will achieve its clean air objective in ways that are appropriate to the Canadian situation and way of doing business. Some of our detractors in the United States say that we have not done it in the American way and question our good faith. To them and to all Members I say, look at the bottom line. Look at the results. Canada has achieved clean air with respect to sulphur dioxide. Now we are taking the action necessary to clean up acid rain.
The transboundary aspects of the acid rain problem can only be solved through the negotiation of a bilateral accord. However, to be effective, to be useful, the accord must call for more than further problem definition and further study. I think most of us are aware that the acid rain problem has been studied to death in the United States. Now is the time for action and control legislation.
The nature, the cause and the solutions to the acid rain problem are already abundantly clear. Unless Canada and the United States can talk about emission control targets and schedules, then we are not talking about a solution, only that the problem exists. One need only open the history books on transboundary environmental issues to see the utility of pollution control targets and schedules. The first Canada-U.S. Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement signed in 1972 contained targets and schedules to reduce phosphorous loading in the lakes. These important waters are healthier today than they were 15 years ago, and improvements continue to be made because of additional targets and schedules in subsequent agreements.
To be acceptable to Canada, a Canada-U.S. acid rain accord must have definite targets and schedules for acid rain reduction. Specifically, the flow of U.S. sulphur dioxide to eastern Canada must be reduced to 2 million tonnes by 1994, a time frame compatible with our own program. I believe that would be about a 50 per cent reduction.
Canada's objective is based on sound scientific information and existing principles and obligations under international law which both Canada and the United States support. Under

international law, states must ensure that activities within their jurisdictions do not cause damage to the environment of other states. This principle was applied in the development of Canada's abatement program, which will reduce the amount of sulphur dioxide that Canada exports to the United States from about 1.5 million tonnes, the 1980 level, to about 800,000 tonnes by 1994.
The United States currently dumps about 3.2 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide on eastern Canada every year, less than the 1980 level of four million tonnes. At least the level is down a bit. As a result of actions taken in the United States, principally to control local air quality, it is already 40 per cent along the course Canada wants it to travel. The federal Government acknowledges that how the United States goes about reducing its transboundary pollution flow to 2 million tonnes is its own business. Canada's interest is in the extent to which transboundary pollution flows are and will be reduced. The federal Government will judge all U.S. initiatives against this yardstick.
The federal Government also acknowledges the realities of the U.S. situation on acid rain. Its regional divisiveness, its potential impact on the high sulphur coal industry, just to mention a couple. We also know that the power to take the necessary action is divided between the executive and the legislative and that these two branches do not always see eye to eye. Indeed, even factions within either branch may not see eye to eye. However, it is up to the United States. It is its obligation to solve them, not Canada's, and to bring the reductions in by 1994.
As a Canadian Member of Parliament with some experience on the acid rain issue, I am forever impressed with the Americans' ability to generate misinformation. The U.S. National Acid Precipitation Assessment Program, commonly known as NAPAP, interim assessment on the causes and effects of acidic deposition is a classic example.
The federal Government has soundly criticized the conclusions of the NAPAP report which can only be described as bizarre in the face of a wealth of conclusive and compelling evidence that has been accumulated on the nature, causes and solutions to the acid rain problem. The executive summary portrays the problem of acid rain as neither serious nor in need of any intervention. It minimizes what is known about the matter, over-complicates what is uncertain and describes a market driven future in unreasonably optimistic terms.
The Minister of the Environment on several occasions has pointed out the flawed, misleading and incomplete nature of the NAPAP report to its U.S. counterpart, to other members of the U.S. administration, the members of the U.S. Congress and to the American people. The Minister has told American decision-makers that scientific information can only assist in public policy making. Science cannot and should not be the sole determinant of public policy. To think so is to put scientific investigation in a role for which it is neither designed nor equipped to do.

The international protocol on the stratospheric ozone depletion, signed in Montreal last September, is an excellent example of the role of science in public policy making. Science gave us the evidence that we had a serious problem with the ozone layer and indications of what is causing the problem, namely, releases of CFCs, chlorofluorocarbons, into the atmosphere. To say we know far more about the science of acid rain than we do about the science of stratospheric ozone depletion is an understatement. Yet the international community, including the United States, was able to band together to slash world-wide releases of CFCs, and Canada played a leadership role in this example of international co-operation to protect the environment.
U.S. decision-makers supported actions to protect the ozone layer. I assure Hon. Members that the Government will continue to make every possible effort to get our American neighbours to accept the need for similar action on acid rain.
The federal Government has a reasoned and reasonable three-pronged strategy for getting U.S. action on acid rain. First, it will continue to work with the U.S. administration. Some Members opposite might ask why we should continue to do so when, despite our best efforts, we have not been very successful to date. The reason is simple and straightforward. If we cannot negotiate with the U.S. Congress, with the American public or with any other American institution, what are we to do?
Second, we will continue to ensure that Congress is fully apprised of the Canadian position. Full and accurate information will be crucial to congressional action on any eventual agreement we conclude with the administration. Members of Congress should have the benefit of our knowledge, research and experience. They should know where we stand and know how important their efforts to reduce U.S. pollution are to the quality of our air and to the acid rain problem.
Third, the federal and provincial Governments and private individuals alike must work with interested Americans in an effort to broadcast the understanding in the United States that acid rain is a serious international problem which must be addressed now. The key to action against acid rain in the United States and in Canada is public opinion.
The Minister of the Environment has personally made contact on more than 45 occasions with Americans to press Canada's case on acid rain, and he plans to do more. Our special committee on acid rain went to Washington last year. We hope to make a further trip this year, and we will certainly be trying to get the message across.
As most Hon. Members know, the Prime Minister and, I assume, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), are going to Washington on April 27. I would hope that the acid rain problem would be very high on their agenda.
I know that free trade is important, but in my view, acid rain is certainly very important.
I might as well tell Hon. Members that I wrote a personal letter to the Prime Minister and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs emphasizing the importance of the acid rain problem. I wrote that we have been nice guys long enough, we must lay it on the line and say that something must be done.
On April 6 of last year, I believe, in this very Chamber, the President of the United States made some comments and gave a half promise that something would be done on acid rain controls. Nothing has been done as yet. Therefore, as I pointed out in my letter to the Prime Minister, on this problem he is on the side of the angels and I would hope that he will certainly lay it on the line.
As I mentioned, the committee will be going there in June, we hope. Arrangements are being made with the embassy. We hope to get the message across so that something will be done.
I understand that there is only a 25 per cent chance, according to experts in Washington, that there will be acid rain legislation this year. I had hoped that the President would go out on a high note by trying to bring in some meaningful legislation on acid rain.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the Hon. Member that I was recently in the Province of Nova Scotia in the vicinity of a thermal-generating station owned by the province which is producing electricity from high sulphur content coal, contributing in our own country to acid rain. It is all very well to say that we all want to see something done on acid rain, but when will the Government take decisive and definitive action, not only to prevent our own industries from contributing to acid rain but to insist that our American counterparts also do their share?
We have put up with an awful lot of nonsense and we have cut back our own commitments. There are no scrubbers on some of our own machinery. When will the Government insist that this be done?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question of the Hon. Member. I am well aware that Nova Scotia produces a great deal of its energy through coal-fired utilities, and I am also well aware that high sulphur content coal is used.
As the Hon. Member may be aware, Nova Scotia was the last province to sign the agreement on pollution. The Hon. Member is also well aware that pollution controls to be put on industry, and this one happens to be a Crown-owned industry, falls under the jurisdiction of the provincial Government. Therefore, it is up to the Province of Nova Scotia to do something. We now have a commitment from the Nova Scotia Government that it will reduce emissions across the board in order to conform and so that Canada will have its emission levels down to 50 per cent of the 1980 level by 1994.
I appreciate what the Hon. Member is saying. There is no question about it, I would like to see that particular utility install scrubbers. I have been a member of acid rain committees for the past seven or eight years, and this fact was thrown
March 21, 1988

in our faces when we went to Washington. We were told: "What are you doing preaching to us when we have scrubbers installed on many of our utilities and you do not have one, and your automobile-emission levels are three times more lenient?"
Now we have rectified that. I am aware that there are no scrubbers and that the only one that may be coming on stream, I believe, is in Ontario. The problem in Canada has been not with our utilities so much as with our smelters. They have been the real cause of the pollution.
A great many of the provinces, Ontario in particular, are moving toward nuclear power which is pollution free, even though it may have certain other dangers. That was one of the reasons why Ontario did not go along with installing scrubbers, even though it had half promised to do so a few years ago.
In Nova Scotia, certainly the great majority of power is produced by means of coal, and I would hope that something will be done on that. The Nova Scotia Government must have some plans since it signed the agreement to make these reductions.
